The meaning: to warn the disbelievers, ﴿and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾, that is, that they will have ﴿a good reward﴾, which is Paradise. ﴿Abiding forever﴾ (*makithina*), (p-104) that is, remaining, and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*). ﴿And to warn﴾ with the punishment of Allah ﴿those who say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾, and they are: the Jews when they said, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," the Christians when they said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and the polytheists when they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." ﴿They have no knowledge of it﴾, that is, of that statement, ﴿nor did their fathers﴾ who said that, ﴿Enormous is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾, that is, it is great in magnitude, ﴿a word﴾.

The majority read it in the accusative (*kalimatan*). Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Abu Razin, Abu Raja', Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ibn Abi Abla read it in the nominative (*kalimatun*). Al-Farra' said: whoever reads it in the accusative has an implied subject: "That word was enormous as a word," and whoever reads it in the nominative does not imply anything, just as you say, "Your saying is great." Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it in the accusative, the meaning is: "Their saying was enormous: 'Allah has taken a son,' as a word," and "a word" is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*). Whoever reads it in the nominative, the meaning is: "It was enormous as a word, which is their saying: 'Allah has taken a son.'"

His saying: ﴿It comes out of their mouths﴾, that is, it is only a statement uttered by the mouth, having no validity and no proof for it. ﴿They say nothing but falsehood﴾, that is, what they say is nothing but falsehood. Then He admonished him for his grief over the loss of what he had hoped for from their acceptance of Islam, and said: ﴿So perhaps you would kill yourself with grief﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Jawza', and Qatadah read *bakhi'un nafsaka* with a kasrah on the sin, as an annexation (*idafah*). The exegetes and linguists said: "perhaps you would destroy yourself, and kill yourself." Abu 'Ubaydah recited for Dhu al-Rummah:

*Alā ayyuhādhā al-bākhi'u al-wajdu nafsahu*
*li-shay'in naḥathatu 'an yadayhi al-maqādiru*

That is: *nahhathathu* (it removed it).

(p-105)

If it is said: How can He say "perhaps" (*la'alla*), when the usual meaning of it is doubt, and Allah knows things before they occur?

The answer: it is not doubt. Rather, it is an implied interrogative used for affirmation (*taqrir*), so the meaning is: "Are you going to kill yourself?" Your grief over their turning away should not extend so far, for whomever We have decreed for wretchedness, regret does not benefit him. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying: ﴿after them﴾, that is, after their turning away from you, ﴿if they do not believe in this statement﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿in grief (*asafan*)﴾. Concerning it there are four sayings:

One: sorrow, said by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Qutaybah. Second: distress, said by Mujahid. Third: anger, said by Qatadah. Fourth: regret, said by al-Suddi. Abu 'Ubaydah said: regret, and anguish, and sorrow. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-asaf* is exaggeration in sorrow or anger. It is said: "The man has become *asif*," and he is *asif*. The poet said:

*Arā rajulan minhum asīfan ka'annamā*
*yaḍummu ilā kashḥayhi kaffan mukhaḍḍaban*

This verse points to the prohibition by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against excessive eagerness for the faith of his people, lest that lead to the destruction of his own self through grief.

(p-102) SURAH AL-KAHF

**Section on its revelation**

Abu Salih related from Ibn Abbas that Surah al-Kahf is Meccan (*Makki*), and likewise said al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatadah. This is the consensus (*ijma'*) of the exegetes (*mufassirun*), with no dispute that we know of, except that it has been narrated from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah that one verse of it is Medinan (*Madani*), namely His saying: ﴿And restrain yourself﴾ (Al-Kahf: 28). Muqatil said: from its beginning up to His saying, ﴿a barren, dusty ground﴾ (Al-Kahf: 8) is Medinan, and His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ (Al-Kahf: 107-108), the two verses, are Medinan, and the rest of it is Meccan.

Abu al-Darda' related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever memorizes the first ten verses of al-Kahf, he will not be harmed by the Dajjal (the Antichrist) if he encounters him. And whoever memorizes the final verses of Surah al-Kahf, they will be a light for him on the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verse 7–8:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have made that which is upon the earth an adornment for it﴾, has four opinions.

The first: that they are men. This was related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that they are the scholars (al-'ulama'), related by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas. According to these two opinions, "ma" is in the place of "min" (of those), because it is in the place of indefiniteness, as stated by Ibn al-Anbari. The third: that it refers to whatever is upon it of things, as stated by Mujahid. The fourth: that it is plants and trees, as stated by Muqatil. The saying of Mujahid is more general, for it includes plants, water, minerals, and other things.

If it is said: We indeed see some of what is upon the earth as ugly and not an adornment.

The answer: If we say that what is meant by it is a specific thing, then the meaning is: We have made some of what is upon the earth an adornment for it. It came in the form of a general statement while its meaning is specific. And if we say that it means men or scholars, then it is for their worship or for their guiding to their Creator. And if we say that it means plants and trees, then it is because it is an adornment for it, functioning as clothing and ornament. And if we say that it is general to all that is upon it, then it is because it indicates its Creator, so in this respect it is the adornment of the earth.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That We may test them﴾; that is, that We may examine creation, and the meaning is: that We may deal with them as one who tests. Ibn al-Anbari said: Whoever says that ﴿what is upon the earth﴾ refers to plants, says the pronoun "hum" (them) and the "mim" return to the inhabitants of the earth who witness the adornment. Whoever says that ﴿what is upon the earth﴾ is men, returns the pronoun "hum" and "mim" to "ma", because it is interpreted as a collective. The meaning of the verse is: that We may test them, so that We see which of them is best in deed, this or that. Al-Hasan said: which of them is most abstinent in the world. We have mentioned four opinions regarding this verse in Surat Hud (7). Then He informed creation that He will annihilate all of that, so He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, We will make what is upon it a barren wasteland (sa'idan juruzan)﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-sa'id is the path on which there is no plant growth. Ibn al-Anbari said: The lexicographers said: al-sa'id is dust and the surface of the earth. As for al-juruz, al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz say "ard juruz" and "juruz", the Asad say "jaraz" and "juruz", and the Tamim say "ard jurz" and "jarz" with lightening. Abu 'Ubayda said: al-sa'id al-juruz is the thick (land) that produces nothing. It is said of a year of drought: juruz, and the plural is sunun ajraz, because of its barrenness and scarcity of rain, and he recited:

"The barren years have swept them away."

Al-Zajjaj said: al-juruz is the land in which nothing grows, as if it eats the plants entirely. Ibn al-Anbari said: The lexicographers said: al-juruz is the land in which no plant remains, burning every plant that is in it. The exegetes said: This will be on the Day of Resurrection, when God will make the earth level, with no plant in it and no water.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verse 9–12 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or did you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were [among] Our signs a wonder?﴾ It was revealed on account of a cause that we have mentioned at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they ask you about the soul﴾ [al-Isra' 85]. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of ﴿Or did you think﴾ is: "Did you think?" As for "al-kahf" (the cave), the exegetes said: it is a cavern in a mountain, but it is wide; if it is small, it is a ghar (a cave, smaller hollow). Ibn al-Anbari said: the philologists said: al-kahf is in the position of the ghar in a mountain.

As for al-raqim (the inscription), there are six sayings concerning it:

The first: it is a tablet of lead in which the names of the youths were written, so that whoever came upon them one day would know their story. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and Wahb ibn Munabbih said likewise, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr in one narration, and Mujahid in one narration. Al-Suddi said: al-Raqim is a rock on which the names of the youths were inscribed, and it was placed in the wall of the city. Muqatil said: al-Raqim is a book written by two righteous men, who were concealing their faith from the king from whom the youths had fled. They wrote the affair of the youths on a tablet of lead, then placed it in a chest of copper, then placed it in the structure with which they had sealed the entrance of the cave, and said: "Perhaps God will make someone come upon these youths, and they will know their affair when they read the book." Al-Farra' said: on the tablet were written their names, their lineages, their religion, and whence they were. Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah said: al-Raqim means the writing; it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and from it comes "kitab marqum," i.e., written.

The second: it is the name of the town from which they went out, said by Ka'b.

The third: it is the name of the mountain, said by al-Hasan and 'Atiyyah.

The fourth: that al-Raqim is the inkwell, in the language of the Romans, said by 'Ikrimah, and Mujahid in one narration.

The fifth: it is the name of the dog, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The sixth: it is the name of the valley in which the cave is, said by Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They were among Our signs a wonder﴾. The exegetes said: the meaning of the speech is: "Did you think that they were the most wondrous of Our signs? Among Our signs there is what is more wondrous than them, for the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them is more wondrous than their story." Ibn Abbas said: what We have given you of the Book, the Sunnah and knowledge is better than their affair.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When the youths sought refuge﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of awaw ilayhi is: they went to it and made it their refuge. "Al-fityah" is the plural of fata, like ghulam and ghilmah, and sabi and sibyah; and "fi'lah" is among the forms of collective nouns, and it is not a pattern that is analogized upon: ghurab and ghirbah are not permissible, nor ghani and ghinyah. Some exegetes said: al-fityah means the young men. We have already mentioned from al-Qutayabi that fata means the complete man among men, and we explained this in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿of your believing young women﴾ [al-Nisa' 25].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they said: Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself﴾; i.e., from Your presence, ﴿mercy﴾; i.e., provision, ﴿and prepare for us﴾; i.e., set right for us, ﴿from our affair a right course﴾; i.e., guide us to that which brings us near to You. The meaning: prepare for us from our affair that by which we attain right guidance. "Al-rushd," "al-rashd," and "al-rashad" are the opposite of error.

Summary of the story of the companions of the cave.

The scholars differed concerning the beginning of their affair and the cause of their coming to the cave, in three sayings:

The first: they fled by night from their king when he called them to worship idols, and they passed by a shepherd who had a dog, and it followed them in their religion. They took refuge in the cave to worship, and one of them would buy their provisions from the city, until one day he came to them and informed them that they had been mentioned, so they wept and sought refuge in God from the trial. God struck upon their ears, and the king ordered that the cave be sealed over them, while he thought they were awake; in fact God had taken their souls in the manner of sleep, and their dog had been overtaken by what had overtaken them. Then the two believing men, who concealed their faith, wrote their names, lineages, and account on a tablet of lead, and placed it in a copper chest in the building, and said: "Perhaps God will make a believing people come upon them, and they will know their account." This is the saying of Ibn Abbas. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: their people lost them and sought them, but God blinded their affair from them, so they wrote their names and lineages on a tablet: "So-and-so and so-and-so, sons of our kings, we lost them in the month of such-and-such, in the year of such-and-such, in the kingdom of so-and-so," and they placed the tablet in the king's treasury, and said: "This will have a matter."

The second: one of the disciples (al-hawariyyun) came to the city of the companions of the cave and wished to enter it, but he was told: "At its gate is an idol; no one enters it without prostrating to it." He disliked entering it, so he went to a bath near the city, where he worked for wages. A group of youths from the people of the city attached themselves to him, and he began to inform them of news of the heavens and the earth and news of the Hereafter, and they believed him and affirmed him. Until one day the king's son came with a woman and entered the bath with her; the disciple denounced this to him, so he reviled him and entered, and he died, and the woman died in the bath. The king came, and it was said to him: "The owner of the bath has killed your son." He was sought, but he fled. The king said: "Who used to accompany him?" The youths were named to him, and they were sought, and they went out of the city. They passed by a companion of theirs in a field, who was in the same condition as they were; he set off with them, and with him a dog, until night overtook them at the cave. They entered it and said: "We will spend the night here, then we will rise in the morning, God willing, and you will see your opinion." God struck upon their ears and they slept. The king and his companions went out following them, and found that they had entered the cave; whenever a man wished to enter the cave, he was struck with terror. One of them said to the king: "Did you not say: if I overpower them, I will kill them?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then wall up the gate of the cave over them, until they die of hunger and thirst." He did so. This is the saying of Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The third: they were sons of the nobles and chiefs of the city; they went out and gathered behind the city without prior appointment. One man among them, the eldest, said: "I find in myself something that I do not think anyone else finds." They said: "What do you find?" He said: "I find in myself that my Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." So they all stood up and said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth," and they agreed to enter the cave; they entered and remained there for what God willed. This is the saying of Mujahid. Qatadah said: they were sons of the kings of the Romans, who singled themselves out with their religion in the cave, so God struck upon their ears.

Section.

The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 18, verses 9–12 (part 2 of 2):

As for the cause of the awakening of the People of the Cave from their sleep, ʿIkrimah said: A believing community (ummah) came, and their king was a believer. They disagreed about the soul and the body. One said: God will resurrect the soul and the body. Another said: He will resurrect only the soul, while the body will be eaten by the earth and will become nothing. Their disagreement troubled the king. So he went, put on coarse woolen garments (masuh), sat on ashes, and called upon God to send them a sign that would make the matter clear to them. Then God raised the People of the Cave.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: A shepherd whom the rain had overtaken came to the cave and said: "If only I could open this cave and let my sheep in out of the rain." He kept working at it until he opened it. God returned their souls to them when they awoke on the following morning.

Ibn al-Sa'ib said: The owner of the land in which the cave lay needed to build a pen (hazirah) for his sheep, so he tore down that barrier and built with its stones, and the door of the cave was opened.

Ibn Ishaq said: God put into the mind of a man from the people of the town that he should demolish that structure and build a pen for his sheep with it. So he hired two workers to remove those stones. They removed them and opened the door of the cave. They sat down joyfully, and they greeted one another, seeing nothing in their faces or bodies that they disliked; they were in the same state in which they had fallen asleep. They thought that their king was searching for them. They prayed, and they said to Yamlikha, the keeper of their provisions (nafaqah): "Go out and listen to what is being said about us, and seek food for us." So he put down his clothes, took the garments in which he used to disguise himself, and went out. He saw that the stones had been removed from the door of the cave, and he was amazed. Then he passed by, hiding himself and fearful that someone would see him and take him to the king. When he saw the gate of the city, he saw upon it a sign that belongs to the people of faith, and he was amazed. It seemed to him that this was not the city he knew, and he saw people whom he did not recognize. He began to wonder and say: "Perhaps I am asleep." When he entered it, he saw people swearing by the name of ʿIsa (Jesus). He stood, leaning his back against a wall, and said to himself: "By God, I do not know what this is. Last evening there was no one on the face of the earth who mentioned ʿIsa except that he was killed, and today I hear them mentioning him. Perhaps this is not the city I know. By God, I do not know any city near our city." He stood like one bewildered. He took out a silver coin (waraq) and gave it to a man, saying: "Sell me food." The man looked at its design and was amazed. Then he handed it to another, and they kept passing it among themselves, wondering and consulting one another. They said: "This man has found a treasure." He became frightened of them and thought that they had recognized it. He said: "Keep your food; I have no need of it." They said to him: "Who are you, young man? By God, you have found a treasure and you want to hide it. Share it with us, or we will bring you to the sultan, and he will kill you." He did not know what to say, so they threw his cloak around his neck while he wept and said: "I have been separated from my brothers. If only they knew what I have suffered." The first: as a verbal noun (masdar); the meaning is: you count a counting.

The second: that it is a description (naʿt) of the years; the meaning is: years of a number (sinin dhat ʿadad). The benefit of mentioning the number of the counted thing is to emphasize the abundance of the thing, because if it is few, its quantity is understood; and if it is many, one needs to count the large number.

﴿Then We raised them﴾ from their sleep. Whoever comes out from death to life, or from sleep to waking, is called "mab'uth" (raised), because what had been holding him back from acting and moving has gone from him. It has also been said: The meaning of ﴿years of a number﴾ is that there were no months or days in them; they were complete years. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So that We might know which of the two parties﴾. The exegetes said: "Ayyu" here means "that We might see." Some of them said: The meaning is: that you yourselves might know. Abu al-Jawza, Abu ʿImran, and al-Nakhaʿi read (liyaʿlama) with a dammah on the yaʾ, in the passive form, so that "ayyu al-hizbayn" is the subject. It seems that there was a dispute among them about the length of their stay in the cave after they had left among themselves, so God raised them to clarify and manifest that. Qatadah said: Neither of the two parties had knowledge of their stay, neither their believers nor their disbelievers. Muqatil said: When they were raised, the doubt disappeared and the reality of their stay became known. Qadi Abu Yaʿla said: The meaning of the statement is: We raised them so that what was known might become manifest in the difference between the two parties about the length of their stay, because in that there is a lesson.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verse 9–12 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or did you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were [among] Our signs a wonder?﴾ It was revealed on account of a cause that we have mentioned at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they ask you about the soul﴾ [al-Isra' 85]. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of ﴿Or did you think﴾ is: "Did you think?" As for "al-kahf" (the cave), the exegetes said: it is a cavern in a mountain, but it is wide; if it is small, it is a ghar (a cave, smaller hollow). Ibn al-Anbari said: the philologists said: al-kahf is in the position of the ghar in a mountain.

As for al-raqim (the inscription), there are six sayings concerning it:

The first: it is a tablet of lead in which the names of the youths were written, so that whoever came upon them one day would know their story. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and Wahb ibn Munabbih said likewise, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr in one narration, and Mujahid in one narration. Al-Suddi said: al-Raqim is a rock on which the names of the youths were inscribed, and it was placed in the wall of the city. Muqatil said: al-Raqim is a book written by two righteous men, who were concealing their faith from the king from whom the youths had fled. They wrote the affair of the youths on a tablet of lead, then placed it in a chest of copper, then placed it in the structure with which they had sealed the entrance of the cave, and said: "Perhaps God will make someone come upon these youths, and they will know their affair when they read the book." Al-Farra' said: on the tablet were written their names, their lineages, their religion, and whence they were. Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah said: al-Raqim means the writing; it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and from it comes "kitab marqum," i.e., written.

The second: it is the name of the town from which they went out, said by Ka'b.

The third: it is the name of the mountain, said by al-Hasan and 'Atiyyah.

The fourth: that al-Raqim is the inkwell, in the language of the Romans, said by 'Ikrimah, and Mujahid in one narration.

The fifth: it is the name of the dog, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The sixth: it is the name of the valley in which the cave is, said by Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They were among Our signs a wonder﴾. The exegetes said: the meaning of the speech is: "Did you think that they were the most wondrous of Our signs? Among Our signs there is what is more wondrous than them, for the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them is more wondrous than their story." Ibn Abbas said: what We have given you of the Book, the Sunnah and knowledge is better than their affair.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When the youths sought refuge﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of awaw ilayhi is: they went to it and made it their refuge. "Al-fityah" is the plural of fata, like ghulam and ghilmah, and sabi and sibyah; and "fi'lah" is among the forms of collective nouns, and it is not a pattern that is analogized upon: ghurab and ghirbah are not permissible, nor ghani and ghinyah. Some exegetes said: al-fityah means the young men. We have already mentioned from al-Qutayabi that fata means the complete man among men, and we explained this in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿of your believing young women﴾ [al-Nisa' 25].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they said: Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself﴾; i.e., from Your presence, ﴿mercy﴾; i.e., provision, ﴿and prepare for us﴾; i.e., set right for us, ﴿from our affair a right course﴾; i.e., guide us to that which brings us near to You. The meaning: prepare for us from our affair that by which we attain right guidance. "Al-rushd," "al-rashd," and "al-rashad" are the opposite of error.

Summary of the story of the companions of the cave.

The scholars differed concerning the beginning of their affair and the cause of their coming to the cave, in three sayings:

The first: they fled by night from their king when he called them to worship idols, and they passed by a shepherd who had a dog, and it followed them in their religion. They took refuge in the cave to worship, and one of them would buy their provisions from the city, until one day he came to them and informed them that they had been mentioned, so they wept and sought refuge in God from the trial. God struck upon their ears, and the king ordered that the cave be sealed over them, while he thought they were awake; in fact God had taken their souls in the manner of sleep, and their dog had been overtaken by what had overtaken them. Then the two believing men, who concealed their faith, wrote their names, lineages, and account on a tablet of lead, and placed it in a copper chest in the building, and said: "Perhaps God will make a believing people come upon them, and they will know their account." This is the saying of Ibn Abbas. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: their people lost them and sought them, but God blinded their affair from them, so they wrote their names and lineages on a tablet: "So-and-so and so-and-so, sons of our kings, we lost them in the month of such-and-such, in the year of such-and-such, in the kingdom of so-and-so," and they placed the tablet in the king's treasury, and said: "This will have a matter."

The second: one of the disciples (al-hawariyyun) came to the city of the companions of the cave and wished to enter it, but he was told: "At its gate is an idol; no one enters it without prostrating to it." He disliked entering it, so he went to a bath near the city, where he worked for wages. A group of youths from the people of the city attached themselves to him, and he began to inform them of news of the heavens and the earth and news of the Hereafter, and they believed him and affirmed him. Until one day the king's son came with a woman and entered the bath with her; the disciple denounced this to him, so he reviled him and entered, and he died, and the woman died in the bath. The king came, and it was said to him: "The owner of the bath has killed your son." He was sought, but he fled. The king said: "Who used to accompany him?" The youths were named to him, and they were sought, and they went out of the city. They passed by a companion of theirs in a field, who was in the same condition as they were; he set off with them, and with him a dog, until night overtook them at the cave. They entered it and said: "We will spend the night here, then we will rise in the morning, God willing, and you will see your opinion." God struck upon their ears and they slept. **Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 18, verses 13–15:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We relate to you their story in truth﴾; that is, the account of the youths, ﴿in truth﴾; that is, with accuracy.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾; that is, We made them steadfast in faith. ﴿And We fortified their hearts﴾; that is, We inspired them with patience, ﴿when they stood up﴾ before their king, Diqyanus, ﴿and said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth."﴾ This was because he used to call the people to worship idols, so God protected these youths until they disobeyed their king. Al-Hasan said: they stood up among their people and called them to tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). It was also said: this was their statement among themselves when they gathered outside the city, as we mentioned at the beginning of the story. As for ﴿shatat﴾, it means injustice. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said "shatta al-rajul" and "ashatta" when a man acts unjustly.

Then the youths said: ﴿These are our people; they have taken besides Him gods﴾; they mean those who lived in the time of Diqyanus. ﴿They have taken gods besides Him﴾; that is, they worshipped idols. ﴿Why do they not bring for them﴾; that is, "why would they not" (lawla means "hallā"), ﴿for them﴾; that is, for the worship of idols, ﴿a clear authority﴾; that is, a clear proof. He said "for them" (ʿalayhim) although the idols are feminine, because the disbelievers attributed to them intellect and discernment, so they were treated as masculine humans.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates against God a lie﴾, by claiming that He has a partner.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 18, verses 13–15:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We relate to you their story in truth﴾; that is, the account of the youths, ﴿in truth﴾; that is, with accuracy.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾; that is, We made them steadfast in faith. ﴿And We fortified their hearts﴾; that is, We inspired them with patience, ﴿when they stood up﴾ before their king, Diqyanus, ﴿and said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth."﴾ This was because he used to call the people to worship idols, so God protected these youths until they disobeyed their king. Al-Hasan said: they stood up among their people and called them to tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). It was also said: this was their statement among themselves when they gathered outside the city, as we mentioned at the beginning of the story. As for ﴿shatat﴾, it means injustice. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said "shatta al-rajul" and "ashatta" when a man acts unjustly.

Then the youths said: ﴿These are our people; they have taken besides Him gods﴾; they mean those who lived in the time of Diqyanus. ﴿They have taken gods besides Him﴾; that is, they worshipped idols. ﴿Why do they not bring for them﴾; that is, "why would they not" (lawla means "hallā"), ﴿for them﴾; that is, for the worship of idols, ﴿a clear authority﴾; that is, a clear proof. He said "for them" (ʿalayhim) although the idols are feminine, because the disbelievers attributed to them intellect and discernment, so they were treated as masculine humans.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates against God a lie﴾, by claiming that He has a partner.

﴿And when you have withdrawn from them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: this is the statement of Yamlikha, who was the leader of the People of the Cave. He said to them, "And when you have withdrawn from them," meaning: you have parted from them, referring to the worshippers of idols. "And what they worship other than Allah" has two interpretations:

The first: "and you have withdrawn from what they worship besides Allah." The people used to worship Allah and also worship other gods alongside Him. The youths withdrew from worshipping the gods but did not withdraw from worshipping Allah. This is the view of 'Ata' al-Khurasani and al-Farra'.

The second: "and what they worship other than Allah." Qatada said: in the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads: "and what they worship instead of Allah," and this is its explanation.

﴿So take refuge in the cave﴾: that is, make it your shelter. ﴿Your Lord will spread for you of His mercy﴾: that is, He will extend to you of His provision. ﴿And will prepare for you from your affair something of ease﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read مِرْفَقًا (mirfaqan) with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa'. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read مَرْفِقًا (marfiqan) with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the fa'. Al-Farra' said: the people of the Hijaz say مَرْفِقًا (marfiqan) with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the fa' for any means by which one is aided, and they use a kasra on the mim of مِرْفَق (mirfaq) for the human elbow, while the Arabs may use a kasra on the mim in both. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of the verse is: "and will prepare for you, in place of your difficult affair, something of ease." The poet said:

"Would that we had, from the water of Zamzam, a drink, cooled, that had spent the night in Tahyan."

Its meaning: would that we had, in place of the water of Zamzam, [such a drink]. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿and will prepare for you﴾: what you fear from the king and his oppression will be made easy for you, and He will bring you ease, gentleness and kindness.

﴿And you would see the sun when it rises﴾: the meaning is, if you had seen it, you would have seen what we have described. ﴿Inclining away (tazawaru)﴾: Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read تَزّاوَرُ (tazzawaru) with a shadda on the zay. 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read تَزاوَرُ (tazawaru) without a shadda. Ibn 'Amir read تَزْوَرُّ (tazwarru), like تَحْمَرُّ (tahmarru). Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Mijlaz, Abu Raja' and al-Jahdari read تَزْوارُّ (tazwarru) with a sukun on the zay, an elongated alif after the waw without a hamza, and a shadda on the ra'. Abu al-Jawza' and Abu al-Sammak read تَزَوَّرُ (tazawwaru) with a fatha on the ta' and the zay, and a shadda on the waw that is fatha-ed, with a light ra', like تُكَوَّرُ (tukawwaru); that is, it inclines and turns. The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 18, verse 18:

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And you would think them awake﴾; that is, if you saw them, you would think them awake. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Ayqaz (the wakeful) are those who are alert. Its singular is yaqit and yaqzan, and the plural is ayqaz. And al-Ruqud are those asleep. Al-Farra' said: the singular of al-Ayqaz is yaqudh and yaqidh. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: they are thought to be awake only because their eyes are open while they are asleep. It was also said: it is because of their turning right and left. Some scholars of knowledge mentioned that the wisdom in keeping their eyes open is that, had their eyelids remained closed, they would have melted away.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We turn them﴾. Abu Raja' recited (wa-tuqallibuhum) with an open taa', a sukun on the qaf, and a light lam with a kasra. Abu al-Jawza' and Ikrima recited (wa-nuqallibuhum) in the same way, except with a nun. ﴿To the right and to the left﴾; that is, on their right sides and on their left sides. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were turned twice each year, six months on this side and six months on that side, so that the earth would not consume their flesh. Mujahid said: they were on one side for three hundred years, then they were turned for nine years. (p-119)

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And their dog stretched out its forelegs at the threshold﴾. He informed that the dog was in the same state as them in sleep, and in appearance it was awake. Regarding "al-Wasid" (the threshold) there are four opinions:

The first: it is the courtyard of the cave. Ibn Abi Talha narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada and al-Farra' said the same. Al-Farra' said: it is said al-Wasid and al-Asid are two dialects, like al-Ikhaf and al-Wikaf, and arrakhtu al-kitab and warrakhtu, and wakkadtu al-amr and akkadtu. The people of the Hijaz say al-Wasid, and the people of Najd say al-Asid, and it means the enclosure and the courtyard.

The second: it is the door. Ikrima narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Suddi said the same. Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning would then be: "and their dog stretched out its forelegs at the door." The poet said:

"In a wide land whose wilderness is not closed to me, and my acquaintance there is not unknown."

The third: it is the earth, which is the dust. al-Awfi narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid, in one narration from them both, said the same.

The fourth: it is the threshold of the door. Ata' said this. Ibn Qutayba said: this is more pleasing to me, because they say "awsid babaka," meaning close your door; that is, shut it. From this is His words: ﴿Indeed it will be closed over them﴾ [al-Humazah: 8]; that is, sealed and shut. Its origin is that you press the door against the threshold when you shut it. What clarifies this is that if you make the dog in the courtyard, it would be outside the cave, but if you make it at the threshold of the door, it could be inside the cave. And although the cave has no door and threshold, what is meant is that the dog is in the place of the threshold of the house, and this is used figuratively.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿If you had looked upon them﴾ [al-A'mash and Abu Husayn recited (law-ittalaʿta) with a damma on the waw (law-ittalaʿtu)] (p-120), ﴿you would have turned from them in flight﴾, out of fear of them. ﴿And you would have been filled﴾: Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited (wa-lamuli'ta) with a light and hamzated form. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' recited (wa-lamullita) with a shadda and hamza. ﴿With terror﴾; that is, fright and fear, because Allah Exalted restrained them with terror so that no one would approach them. It was also said: their hair and nails had grown extremely long, so whoever saw them would flee in terror, as al-Zajjaj related.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verses 19–20:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We raised them﴾; that is, just as We did to them what We have mentioned, We raised them from that sleep. ﴿So that they might question one another﴾; that is, so that there would be among them questioning, disputing, and disagreement about the length of their stay, and their questioning would benefit those who take heed by considering their condition. ﴿A speaker among them said: "How long have you remained?"﴾; that is, how much time has passed for us since we entered this cave? ﴿They said: "We have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ That is because they had entered in the early morning, and Allah raised them at the end of the day. Therefore they said "a day," and when they saw the sun, they said "or part of a day." ﴿They said: "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained."﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: The one who said this was Yamlikha, their leader, who referred the knowledge of that to Allah, may He be exalted. In another narration he said: It was said by Maksilmina, and he was the eldest of them. Abu Sulayman said: This implies that their own souls had told them that they had remained longer than they mentioned. It has also been said: They only said that because they saw that their nails and hair had grown very long.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So send one of you﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: He said "ahadakum" (one of you) and did not say "wahidukum" (your single one), so that the meaning would not be confused with the praised and exalted one, for the Arabs say "I saw one (ahad) of the people," and do not say "I saw the one (wahid) of the people," except when they intend to honor him. So by "one of them" he meant some of them, not their noble one.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿with your silver﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read it as "biwariqikum" with the ra vowelled with a kasra and lightened. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read it with the ra sukun (unvowelled). And on the authority of Abu 'Amr, it is read as "biwariqikum" assimilated (idgham), with a slight hint of heaviness (tathqil). Al-Zajjaj said: It becomes a pure kaf. Al-Farra' said: "al-waraq" is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, while Tamim say "al-waraq," and some of the Arabs vowel the waw with a kasra, saying "al-wiriq." Ibn Qutayba said: "al-waraq" is silver, whether in dirhams or otherwise. This is shown by the hadith of 'Arfaja that he made a nose from silver (waraq).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to the city﴾; they mean the one from which they had come out. Its name was Daqsus, and it is said that today it is called Tarsus.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿let him look to see which of them has the purest food﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: which of its people. ﴿has the purest food﴾. The commentators have six opinions regarding its meaning:

The first: the most lawful slaughtered meat. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata', because most of the people of their city were disbelievers, who slaughtered for the idols (tawaghit), while among them were some people who concealed their faith. The second: the most lawful food, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Dahhak said: Most of their wealth was usurped. Mujahid said: They said to their companion: Do not buy food in which there is injustice or usurpation. The third: the most abundant, said by 'Ikrima. The fourth: the best (khayr), i.e., the finest, said by Qatada. The fifth: the purest (atyab), said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil. The sixth: the cheapest, said by Yaman ibn Rayyab. Ibn Qutayba said: The root of zakah (purification, growth) is growth and increase.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so let him bring you provision from it﴾; that is, with what you eat. ﴿and let him be gentle﴾; that is, let him examine it carefully and be discreet, so that no one notices him. ﴿and let him not make anyone aware of you﴾; that is, let no one inform anyone of your whereabouts. ﴿For if they come upon you﴾; that is, if they discover you and gain sight of you, ﴿they will stone you﴾. In this there are three opinions:

The first: they will kill you, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: They will kill you by stoning. The second: they will stone you with their hands, out of disapproval of you, said by al-Hasan. The third: they will stone you with their tongues, by insulting you, said by Mujahid and Ibn Juraij.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or return you to their religion﴾; that is, they will bring you back into their religion. ﴿and you will never succeed then, ever﴾; that is, if you return to their religion, you will not be made happy in this world or in the Hereafter.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so let him bring you provision from it﴾; that is, with what you eat. ﴿and let him be gentle﴾; that is, let him examine it carefully and be discreet, so that no one notices him. ﴿and let him not make anyone aware of you﴾; that is, let no one inform anyone of your whereabouts. ﴿For if they come upon you﴾; that is, if they discover you and gain sight of you, ﴿they will stone you﴾. In this there are three opinions:

The first: they will kill you, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: They will kill you by stoning. The second: they will stone you with their hands, out of disapproval of you, said by al-Hasan. The third: they will stone you with their tongues, by insulting you, said by Mujahid and Ibn Juraij.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or return you to their religion﴾; that is, they will bring you back into their religion. ﴿and you will never succeed then, ever﴾; that is, if you return to their religion, you will not be made happy in this world or in the Hereafter.

And so We made them known to the people (lit. "We caused them to be discovered") — i.e., just as We put them to sleep and raised them up, We caused them to become known and manifest to others.

Ibn Qutayba said: The origin of this is that whoever stumbles upon something while being heedless, looks at it until he recognizes it. So the word ʿithār (stumbling upon) was borrowed in place of tabayyun (becoming clear) and ẓuhūr (becoming manifest). From it is the saying of people: "I never stumbled upon (ʿathartu ʿalā) so-and-so doing anything bad," i.e., I never came to know that of him.

Regarding His words, ﴿so that they might know﴾: concerning those to whom this knowledge was made known, there are two views:

The first: they are the people of their town at the time they disputed about the Resurrection. So God raised up the People of the Cave so that they would know ﴿that the promise of God﴾ of resurrection and recompense ﴿is true﴾, and that the Hour has no doubt in it. This is the view of the majority.

The second: they are the People of the Cave themselves. We raised them so that they would see, after their knowledge, that the promise of God is true. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His words, ﴿when they disputed among themselves﴾: meaning the people of that time. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is "when they were disputing," and it may also mean "when they disputed."

As for what they disputed about, there are five views:

One: they disputed about the building and the mosque. The Muslims said: "We shall build a mosque over them, since they are upon our religion." The polytheists said: "We shall build a structure over them, since they are of our way." This was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they disputed about resurrection. The Muslims said: bodies and spirits will be resurrected; some of them said: only spirits will be resurrected, not bodies. So God showed them the resurrection of spirits and bodies through His raising of the People of the Cave. This was reported by ʿIkrima.

The third: they disputed about what to do with the youths. This was reported by Muqatil.

The fourth: they disputed about the length of their stay.

The fifth: they disputed about their number. Al-Tha'labi mentioned these last two.

His words, ﴿Build over them a structure﴾: that is, conceal them from people by placing them behind that structure. Regarding those who said this, there are two views:

One: they were the polytheists of that time, as mentioned above from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they were those who had become Muslims upon seeing the People of the Cave. This was reported by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His words, ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said﴾: Ibn Qutayba said: meaning the authoritative ones and the leaders. The commentators said: they were the king and his believing companions, who took a mosque over them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the king built a church (bay'a) over them.

﴿سَيَقُولُونَ ثَلاثَةٌ﴾ [They will say, "They are three."] Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿ثَلاثَةٌ﴾ is in the nominative as the predicate of the subject (khabar al-ibtida'). The meaning is: "Those who disputed about their affair will say: they are three." There are two opinions regarding these speakers:

The first: they are the Christians of Najran, who debated with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the number of the People of the Cave. The Malkiyyah said: "They are three, the fourth being their dog." The Ya'qubiyyah said: "They are five, the sixth being their dog." The Nestorians said: "They are seven, the eighth being their dog." Then this verse was revealed. Al-Dahhak narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

The second: they are the people of their city before they came to dominate them. Al-Mawardi mentioned this.

﴿رَجْمًا بِالغَيْبِ﴾ [conjecturing about the unseen]: that is, guessing without certainty. Zuhayr said:

War is nothing but what you know and have tasted,
and he is not one to speak of it in conjecture.

As for the presence of the conjunction "and" (wa) in His words ﴿وَثامِنُهم كَلْبُهُمْ﴾ [and the eighth is their dog], while it is absent before this, there are four opinions:

The first: its presence and its absence are equivalent. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: the appearance of the "and" in the eighth clause indicates that it is intended in the two preceding clauses. So by mentioning it here He informs that it is intended before. It was only omitted for lightness. This was mentioned by Abu Nasr in "Sharh al-Luma'".

The third: its presence indicates the end of the narrative and that the speech is complete. This was also mentioned by al-Zajjaj, and it is the view of Muqatil ibn Sulayman. The conjunction "and" indicates the completion of the speech before it and the beginning of what follows. Al-Tha'labi said: "This is the 'and' of judgment and affirmation, as if Allah the Exalted related their disagreement, the speech was complete at His words ﴿وَيَقُولُونَ سَبْعَةٌ﴾ [and they say: seven], then He judged that their eighth is their dog." It is reported in some tafsir that the Muslims said, when the Christians differed: "They are seven," so Allah affirmed the statement of the Muslims.

The fourth: the Arabs join with "and" to the seven, so they say: "six, seven, and eight," because the complete count for them is seven. Like His words: ﴿التّائِبُونَ العابِدُونَ...﴾ [the repentant, the worshippers...] up to His saying in the eighth attribute: ﴿والنّاهُونَ عَنِ المُنْكَرِ﴾ [and those who forbid evil] [al-Tawbah: 112]. And His saying about the attributes of Paradise: ﴿وَفُتِحَتْ أبْوابُها﴾ [and its gates will be opened], and about the attributes of Hell: ﴿فُتِحَتْ أبْوابُها﴾ [its gates have been opened] [al-Zumar: 71-73], because the gates of Hell are seven and the gates of Paradise are eight. Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi mentioned this meaning.

The scholars differed about their number on two opinions:

The first: they were seven. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: they were eight. This was said by Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Ishaq. Ibn al-Anbari said: "It has been said: the meaning of His words ﴿وَثامِنُهم كَلْبُهُمْ﴾ is: their dog's companion, as one says: 'Generosity is Hatim, and poetry is Zuhayr,' i.e., the generosity is the generosity of Hatim, and the poetry is the poetry of Zuhayr."

As for their names, Hushaym said: Maksilmina, Yamlikha, Tarynus, Sadynus, Sarynus, Nawasus, and Yaranus. There is disagreement in the tafsir about their names, so I did not dwell on them.

They differed about to whom their dog belonged, on three opinions:

The first: it belonged to a shepherd whom they passed by, and the shepherd and the dog followed them. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: it belonged to them, and they used it for hunting. This was said by Ubayd ibn Umayr.

The third: they passed by a dog, which followed them, and they drove it away, but it returned. They did this with it several times, then the dog said to them: "What do you want from me? Do not fear my side. I love the beloved of Allah. Sleep, and I will guard you." This was said by Ka'b al-Ahbar.

Regarding the name of their dog there are four opinions:

The first: Qitmir. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.
The second: its name is al-Raqim, which we mentioned from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.
The third: Qatmur. This was said by Abdullah ibn Kathir.
The fourth: Himran. This was said by Shu'ayb al-Jibba'i.

Regarding its description there are three opinions:

The first: it was red. This was related by al-Thawri.
The second: it was yellow. This was related by Ibn Ishaq.
The third: its head was red, its back black, its belly white, and its tail spotted. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

﴿رَبِّي أعْلَمُ بِعِدَّتِهِمْ﴾ [My Lord knows best their number]: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu Amr vocalized the ya' (with a vowel), and the rest made it silent.

﴿ما يَعْلَمُهم إلا قَلِيلٌ﴾ [None knows them except a few]: that is, none knows their number except a few people. Ata' said: "By the few he means the People of the Book." Ibn Abbas said: "I am among that few; they are seven; Allah counted them up to the seven."

﴿فَلا تُمارِ فِيهِمْ إلا مِراءً ظاهِرًا﴾ [So do not argue about them except with an apparent argument]: Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: do not argue with anyone; what I have related to you of their affair is sufficient for you. Ibn Zayd said: do not dispute about their number except with an apparent argument, meaning that you say to them: "It is not as you say; it is not as you know." It has been said: "an apparent argument" means with a clear proof; this was related by al-Mawardi. Al-Mira' in language means disputation. It is said: "Mara yumari muma'atan wa miran," i.e., he disputed. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of the verse is: do not dispute except the dispute of one certain and knowing the reality of the report, since Allah has conveyed to you what no falsehood can touch. The linguistic definition of al-mira' is: drawing out the anger of the disputant, from the saying "maraytu al-shah," when you draw out its milk.

﴿وَلا تَسْتَفْتِ فِيهِمْ﴾ [And do not ask for a ruling about them], i.e., about the People of the Cave, ﴿مِنهُمْ﴾ [from them]. Ibn Abbas said: that is, from the People of the Book. Al-Farra' said: two groups of Christians came to him, a Nestorian and a Ya'qubi, and the Prophet ﷺ asked them about their number, so he was forbidden from that.

﴿وَلا تَقُولَنَّ لِشَيْءٍ إنِّي فاعِلٌ ذَلِكَ غَدًا﴾ [And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow"] ﴿إلا أنْ يَشاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ [unless Allah wills]. The occasion of its revelation: "The Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ about Dhu al-Qarnayn, about the Spirit, and about the People of the Cave. He said: 'Tomorrow I will inform you of that,' and he did not say, 'If Allah wills.' So Jibril delayed for fifteen days because he had left out the exception, and this grieved him. Then this verse was revealed." Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas. The meaning of the speech is: "Do not say of anything: 'I will do that tomorrow,' unless you say: 'If Allah wills.'" So the verb "say" is omitted.

﴿واذْكُرْ رَبَّكَ إذا نَسِيتَ﴾ [And remember your Lord when you forget]. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is: remember your Lord after the forgetting has passed, as you say: "Mention to Abdullah your need when he has prayed," i.e., after the prayer has ended.

The exegetes have three opinions regarding the meaning of the verse:

The first: the meaning is: if you forget the exception and then recall, then say: "If Allah wills," even if it is after a day, a month, or a year. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and the majority.

The second: the meaning of ﴿إذا نَسِيتَ﴾ is: when you become angry. This was said by Ikrimah. Ibn al-Anbari said: this is not far-fetched, because anger produces forgetfulness.

The third: if you forget something, remember Allah so that He reminds you of it. This was related by al-Mawardi.

**Section**

Ibn Kathir read it with a ya' in both states. Ibn Amir, Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read it without a ya' in both states.

There are two opinions regarding the meaning of the speech:

The first: "Perhaps my Lord will give me, from the signs and proofs of prophethood, what will be closer to right guidance and more indicative than the story of the People of the Cave." Allah did that for him and gave him knowledge of the unseen matters of the messengers, which is clearer in proof and closer to right guidance than the report of the People of the Cave. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The second: when the Quraysh asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to inform them of the story of the People of the Cave, he said: "Tomorrow I will inform you," as we explained in the occasion of revelation. So Allah the Exalted said to him: ﴿وَقُلْ عَسى أنْ يَهْدِيَنِي رَبِّي﴾; that is, "Perhaps my Lord will let me know the answer to your questions before the time I set for you, and will hasten for me right guidance from Him." This is the view of Ibn al-Anbari.

﴿سَيَقُولُونَ ثَلاثَةٌ﴾ [They will say, "They are three."] Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿ثَلاثَةٌ﴾ is in the nominative as the predicate of the subject (khabar al-ibtida'). The meaning is: "Those who disputed about their affair will say: they are three." There are two opinions regarding these speakers:

The first: they are the Christians of Najran, who debated with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the number of the People of the Cave. The Malkiyyah said: "They are three, the fourth being their dog." The Ya'qubiyyah said: "They are five, the sixth being their dog." The Nestorians said: "They are seven, the eighth being their dog." Then this verse was revealed. Al-Dahhak narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

The second: they are the people of their city before they came to dominate them. Al-Mawardi mentioned this.

﴿رَجْمًا بِالغَيْبِ﴾ [conjecturing about the unseen]: that is, guessing without certainty. Zuhayr said:

War is nothing but what you know and have tasted,
and he is not one to speak of it in conjecture.

As for the presence of the conjunction "and" (wa) in His words ﴿وَثامِنُهم كَلْبُهُمْ﴾ [and the eighth is their dog], while it is absent before this, there are four opinions:

The first: its presence and its absence are equivalent. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: the appearance of the "and" in the eighth clause indicates that it is intended in the two preceding clauses. So by mentioning it here He informs that it is intended before. It was only omitted for lightness. This was mentioned by Abu Nasr in "Sharh al-Luma'".

The third: its presence indicates the end of the narrative and that the speech is complete. This was also mentioned by al-Zajjaj, and it is the view of Muqatil ibn Sulayman. The conjunction "and" indicates the completion of the speech before it and the beginning of what follows. Al-Tha'labi said: "This is the 'and' of judgment and affirmation, as if Allah the Exalted related their disagreement, the speech was complete at His words ﴿وَيَقُولُونَ سَبْعَةٌ﴾ [and they say: seven], then He judged that their eighth is their dog." It is reported in some tafsir that the Muslims said, when the Christians differed: "They are seven," so Allah affirmed the statement of the Muslims.

The fourth: the Arabs join with "and" to the seven, so they say: "six, seven, and eight," because the complete count for them is seven. Like His words: ﴿التّائِبُونَ العابِدُونَ...﴾ [the repentant, the worshippers...] up to His saying in the eighth attribute: ﴿والنّاهُونَ عَنِ المُنْكَرِ﴾ [and those who forbid evil] [al-Tawbah: 112]. And His saying about the attributes of Paradise: ﴿وَفُتِحَتْ أبْوابُها﴾ [and its gates will be opened], and about the attributes of Hell: ﴿فُتِحَتْ أبْوابُها﴾ [its gates have been opened] [al-Zumar: 71-73], because the gates of Hell are seven and the gates of Paradise are eight. Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi mentioned this meaning.

The scholars differed about their number on two opinions:

The first: they were seven. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: they were eight. This was said by Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Ishaq. Ibn al-Anbari said: "It has been said: the meaning of His words ﴿وَثامِنُهم كَلْبُهُمْ﴾ is: their dog's companion, as one says: 'Generosity is Hatim, and poetry is Zuhayr,' i.e., the generosity is the generosity of Hatim, and the poetry is the poetry of Zuhayr."

As for their names, Hushaym said: Maksilmina, Yamlikha, Tarynus, Sadynus, Sarynus, Nawasus, and Yaranus. There is disagreement in the tafsir about their names, so I did not dwell on them.

They differed about to whom their dog belonged, on three opinions:

The first: it belonged to a shepherd whom they passed by, and the shepherd and the dog followed them. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: it belonged to them, and they used it for hunting. This was said by Ubayd ibn Umayr.

The third: they passed by a dog, which followed them, and they drove it away, but it returned. They did this with it several times, then the dog said to them: "What do you want from me? Do not fear my side. I love the beloved of Allah. Sleep, and I will guard you." This was said by Ka'b al-Ahbar.

Regarding the name of their dog there are four opinions:

The first: Qitmir. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.
The second: its name is al-Raqim, which we mentioned from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.
The third: Qatmur. This was said by Abdullah ibn Kathir.
The fourth: Himran. This was said by Shu'ayb al-Jibba'i.

Regarding its description there are three opinions:

The first: it was red. This was related by al-Thawri.
The second: it was yellow. This was related by Ibn Ishaq.
The third: its head was red, its back black, its belly white, and its tail spotted. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

﴿رَبِّي أعْلَمُ بِعِدَّتِهِمْ﴾ [My Lord knows best their number]: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu Amr vocalized the ya' (with a vowel), and the rest made it silent.

﴿ما يَعْلَمُهم إلا قَلِيلٌ﴾ [None knows them except a few]: that is, none knows their number except a few people. Ata' said: "By the few he means the People of the Book." Ibn Abbas said: "I am among that few; they are seven; Allah counted them up to the seven."

﴿فَلا تُمارِ فِيهِمْ إلا مِراءً ظاهِرًا﴾ [So do not argue about them except with an apparent argument]: Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: do not argue with anyone; what I have related to you of their affair is sufficient for you. Ibn Zayd said: do not dispute about their number except with an apparent argument, meaning that you say to them: "It is not as you say; it is not as you know." It has been said: "an apparent argument" means with a clear proof; this was related by al-Mawardi. Al-Mira' in language means disputation. It is said: "Mara yumari muma'atan wa miran," i.e., he disputed. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of the verse is: do not dispute except the dispute of one certain and knowing the reality of the report, since Allah has conveyed to you what no falsehood can touch. The linguistic definition of al-mira' is: drawing out the anger of the disputant, from the saying "maraytu al-shah," when you draw out its milk.

﴿وَلا تَسْتَفْتِ فِيهِمْ﴾ [And do not ask for a ruling about them], i.e., about the People of the Cave, ﴿مِنهُمْ﴾ [from them]. Ibn Abbas said: that is, from the People of the Book. Al-Farra' said: two groups of Christians came to him, a Nestorian and a Ya'qubi, and the Prophet ﷺ asked them about their number, so he was forbidden from that.

﴿وَلا تَقُولَنَّ لِشَيْءٍ إنِّي فاعِلٌ ذَلِكَ غَدًا﴾ [And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow"] ﴿إلا أنْ يَشاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ [unless Allah wills]. The occasion of its revelation: "The Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ about Dhu al-Qarnayn, about the Spirit, and about the People of the Cave. He said: 'Tomorrow I will inform you of that,' and he did not say, 'If Allah wills.' So Jibril delayed for fifteen days because he had left out the exception, and this grieved him. Then this verse was revealed." Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas. The meaning of the speech is: "Do not say of anything: 'I will do that tomorrow,' unless you say: 'If Allah wills.'" So the verb "say" is omitted.

﴿واذْكُرْ رَبَّكَ إذا نَسِيتَ﴾ [And remember your Lord when you forget]. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is: remember your Lord after the forgetting has passed, as you say: "Mention to Abdullah your need when he has prayed," i.e., after the prayer has ended.

The exegetes have three opinions regarding the meaning of the verse:

The first: the meaning is: if you forget the exception and then recall, then say: "If Allah wills," even if it is after a day, a month, or a year. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and the majority.

The second: the meaning of ﴿إذا نَسِيتَ﴾ is: when you become angry. This was said by Ikrimah. Ibn al-Anbari said: this is not far-fetched, because anger produces forgetfulness.

The third: if you forget something, remember Allah so that He reminds you of it. This was related by al-Mawardi.

**Section**

The benefit of the exception is that the swearer is freed from lying if he does not do what he swore to do. Like His words about the story of Musa: ﴿سَتَجِدُنِي إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ صابِرًا﴾ [You will find me, if Allah wills, patient] [al-Kahf: 69], and he did not remain patient, yet he was spared from lying because the exception was present in his case. The narration from Ahmad is not contradictory: the exception is not valid in divorce (talaq) and manumission (itq); if he says, "You are divorced, if Allah wills," and "You are free, if Allah wills," the divorce takes effect. This is the view of Malik. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: nothing of that takes effect. As for oaths by Allah the Exalted, the exception in them is valid, unlike divorce. Likewise the exception applies to everything that involves expiation, such as zihar and vows, because the wording of divorce and manumission is a wording of effecting. When he attaches the will to it, we know that it has occurred, since the wording of effecting is present on his part. This is unlike the rest of oaths, because they do not necessarily entail a ruling; they are only tied to future actions.

The scholars differed about the time in which the exception is valid, on three opinions:

The first: the exception is valid only when joined to the speech. Something similar has been narrated from Ahmad, and most jurists hold this.

The second: it is valid as long as they are in the same gathering. This was said by al-Hasan and Tawus, and something similar is narrated from Ahmad.

The third: if he makes the exception after a year, it is permissible. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Abu al-'Aliyah. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: "The correct view for a person is to make the exception even after breaking his oath, saying: 'If Allah wills,' so that by this he is freed from what Allah imposed upon him in this verse, and the burden falls from him. As for expiation, it never falls from him in any case, unless the exception is joined to his oath. Whoever said, 'He may make the exception even after a year,' intended the removal of the burden that is imposed on him by leaving out the exception, but not the expiation."

﴿وَقُلْ عَسى أنْ يَهْدِيَنِي رَبِّي﴾ [And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me"]. Nafi' and Abu Amr read "yahdiyanī rabbī" with a ya' in连接 (in continuous recitation) but not in pause. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verse 25–26:

Allah's saying: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read (ثلاثمائةٍ سنينَ) with tanwin (nunation). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (ثلاثمائةِ سنينَ) in the genitive construct, without tanwin. Abu 'Ali said: a numeral added to a singular unit has also come added to a plural collective, as the poet says:

They provided me with nothing but a torn turban, and five hundred of them are bows and counterfeit coins.

There are two views regarding this statement:

The first: it is a report of what the people said about them, and not the exact measure of their stay. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, who argued for it, saying: "Had they remained that long, He would not have said: ﴿Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾." Qatadah also said this, and it is the view of the People of the Book.

The second: it is the exact measure of how long they stayed. This was said by 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. The meaning is: they remained this length from the day they entered it until Allah raised them and made the creation aware of them.

Allah's saying: ﴿years﴾. Al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj said: the implied construction is "years three hundred." Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is that they were not months or days, but were years. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "years" (sinin) is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿three hundred﴾. al-Dahhak said: when ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred﴾ was revealed, they said: days, or months, or years? Then "years" was revealed; therefore He said "years" and did not say "year."

Allah's saying: ﴿And they add nine﴾, meaning nine years. He dispensed with mentioning the years because they had already been mentioned. Then He informed that He knows best the length of their stay, against the People of the Book who differed about it, so He said: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: the Christians of Najran said: as for the three hundred, we know it, but as for the nine we have no knowledge of them. So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾. It was also said: the People of the Book said that for the youths, from the time they entered the cave until this day of ours, is three hundred and nine years. Allah rejected that and said: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾, after He had taken their souls until this day of yours; none knows that but Allah. It was also said: He added the nine because it is the difference between solar years and lunar years, related by al-Mawardi.

Allah's saying: ﴿See how much He sees and hears﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: it is in the manner of exclamation (ta'ajjub), meaning: how much He hears and sees. That is, He knows the story of the People of the Cave and others. This is the view of al-Zajjaj, who mentioned that it is the consensus of the scholars.

The second: it is in the sense of a command, meaning: see by the religion of Allah and hear; that is, see by the guidance of Allah and hear, so the pronoun returns either to the guidance or to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this.

Allah's saying: ﴿They have no protector besides Him﴾; that is, there is no helper for the people of the heavens and the earth apart from Allah. ﴿And He does not share His judgment with anyone﴾. It is not permissible for any judge to rule other than by what He has ruled, and no one may rule by his own self, thereby becoming a partner with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His judgment. Ibn 'Amir read (ولا تُشرِكْ) with a jussive and a ta', and the meaning is: do not associate, O human being.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verses 27–28:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you﴾ (wa-tlu ma ūḥiya ilayka). There are two opinions regarding this recitation:

The first: it means recitation (qirāʾa). The second: it means following (ittibāʿ). The meaning according to the first is: recite the Qur'an; according to the second: follow it and act upon it. We have explained the meaning of ﴿none can alter His words﴾ in (al-Anʿām: 115).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you will not find other than Him a refuge (multaḥad)﴾. Mujahid and al-Farra' said: a refuge (malja'). Al-Zajjaj said: a place to turn away from His command and His prohibition. Others said: a place to which you incline for seeking refuge.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And keep yourself patient (wa-iṣbir nafsaka)﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "The hearts-to-be-reconciled (al-Muallafa qulūbuhum) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn, al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis, and their like, and they said: O Messenger of Allah, if you were to sit at the head of the gathering and push these away from us – they meant: Salman, Abu Dharr, and the poor Muslims, who wore woolen cloaks – we would sit with you and take from you. So this verse was revealed up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire﴾. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) got up seeking them, until he found them at the back of the mosque remembering Allah. He said: 'Praise be to Allah who did not take me until He commanded me to keep myself patient with men of my Ummah. Your life is with you and your death is with you.'" This is the saying of Salman al-Farisi.

The meaning of His saying: (p-133) ﴿keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾; i.e., restrain yourself with them upon performing the prayers ﴿morning and evening﴾. We have explained this verse in (al-Anʿām: 52) up to His saying: ﴿and let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾; i.e., do not turn your gaze to others of the people of wealth and nobility. He, peace be upon him, was keen upon the faith of the leaders so that their followers would believe, and he never desired the adornment of this world at all, so he was commanded to make his attention directed to the poor believers.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾. The occasion of its revelation: Umayya ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to drive away the poor from him and to bring near the chieftains of the people of Makkah, so this verse was revealed. Al-Dahhak narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas. In another narration from him he said: it is ʿUyayna and his like. The meaning of ﴿We have made heedless his heart (aghfalnā qalbahu)﴾: We made it heedless. Abu Mijlaz recited: "man aghfalnā" with a fatḥa on the lām and raising the bāʾ of "qalb". ﴿from Our remembrance﴾: from the Tawhid, the Qur'an and Islam; ﴿and he followed his desire﴾ in polytheism. ﴿and his affair was furuṭ (excess/neglect)﴾. Concerning it there are four opinions:

The first: he exceeded in his speech, for he said: "We are the heads of Mudar; if we become Muslim, the people will become Muslim after us." This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: loss (ḍayāʿ), said by Mujahid. Abu ʿUbayda said: extravagance and waste. The third: regret (nadaman), related by Ibn Qutayba from Abu ʿUbayda. The fourth: his affair was tafrīṭ (negligence), and tafrīṭ is the putting forward of incapacity, said by al-Zajjaj.
