His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾. The occasion of its revelation: Umayya ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to drive away the poor from him and to bring near the chieftains of the people of Makkah, so this verse was revealed. Al-Dahhak narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas. In another narration from him he said: it is ʿUyayna and his like. The meaning of ﴿We have made heedless his heart (aghfalnā qalbahu)﴾: We made it heedless. Abu Mijlaz recited: "man aghfalnā" with a fatḥa on the lām and raising the bāʾ of "qalb". ﴿from Our remembrance﴾: from the Tawhid, the Qur'an and Islam; ﴿and he followed his desire﴾ in polytheism. ﴿and his affair was furuṭ (excess/neglect)﴾. Concerning it there are four opinions:

The first: he exceeded in his speech, for he said: "We are the heads of Mudar; if we become Muslim, the people will become Muslim after us." This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: loss (ḍayāʿ), said by Mujahid. Abu ʿUbayda said: extravagance and waste. The third: regret (nadaman), related by Ibn Qutayba from Abu ʿUbayda. The fourth: his affair was tafrīṭ (negligence), and tafrīṭ is the putting forward of incapacity, said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verse 29:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: Say that which I have brought you is the truth from your Lord.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever wills - let him believe; and whoever wills - let him disbelieve﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

The first: "Whoever Allah wills, let him believe." This was narrated from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is a threat and a warning, not a command. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: that its meaning is: You do not benefit Allah by your faith, nor do you harm Him by your disbelief. This was said by al-Mawardi. Some of them said: This is a display of independence (from you), not a permission for disbelief.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared﴾; i.e., We have readied and prepared. We have explained it in His saying: ﴿And prepared for them a reclining couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. As for "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimun), the exegetes said: they are the disbelievers. As for "the enclosure" (al-suradiq), al-Zajjaj said: al-suradiq is everything that surrounds a thing, such as the cloth partition in a tent, or the wall that encloses a thing. Ibn Qutayba said: al-suradiq is the chamber that is around the tent (fustat). I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur the linguist, who said: al-suradiq is a Persian word that has been Arabized, and its origin in Persian is sardar, which is the vestibule. Al-Farazdaq said:

"I wished for them, until when I met them, I left for them, before the striking, the suradiq."

Regarding the intended meaning of this suradiq there are two opinions:

The first: that it is a suradiq of fire. This was said by Ibn Abbas. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The enclosure of the Fire has four walls, thick, each wall of which is a distance of forty years." And in the narration of Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, he said: (p-135) The suradiq is a tongue of fire, which emerges from the Fire and encompasses them until the reckoning of them is finished.

The second: that it is a smoke that encompasses the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, which is the shadow with three branches that Allah mentioned in (al-Mursalat: 30). This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they call for relief﴾; i.e., from what they are in of torment and intense thirst, ﴿they will be relieved with water like molten brass﴾. Concerning this there are seven opinions:

The first: that it is thick water like the dregs of oil. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is anything that has been melted until it has dissolved. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. Abu Ubayda and al-Zajjaj said: anything you melt of copper, lead, or the like is called muhl.

The third: pus and black blood like the sediment of oil. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: that it is silver and lead that are melted. This was also narrated from Mujahid.

The fifth: that it is that whose heat has ended. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The sixth: [that it is] the pus. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned it. Mughith ibn Sumayy said: This water is what flows from the sweat of the people of the standing place on the Last Day and their weeping, and what flows from them of blood and pus; it flows into a valley in Hell, and Hell cooks it, and it will be the first thing with which the people of the Fire are relieved.

The seventh: that it is the ash that is shaken off a loaf when it comes out of the oven. Ibn al-Anbari related it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It scalds the faces﴾. The exegetes said: when it is brought near to him, the skin of his face falls off into it. Then He condemned it, saying: ﴿Wretched is the drink, and evil is the Fire as a resting place (murtafaqa)﴾. Concerning this there are five opinions:

The first: a dwelling place, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: a gathering place, said by Mujahid. The third: a reclining couch, said by Abu Ubayda, who recited for Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Indeed I stayed awake, so I spent the night reclining (murtafiqan), as if in my eyes is bitter aloes, slaughtered."

Its "dhabh" (slaughter) is its bursting forth. Al-Zajjaj said: "murtafiqan" is in the accusative as a specification, and the meaning of murtafiqan is: reclining upon the elbow. The fourth: it is evil as a sitting place, said by Ibn Qutayba. The fifth: it is evil as a place sought for ease; because whoever seeks ease from it will not find it, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. The meanings of these sayings are close, and the root of "mirfaq" in the language is: that by which one seeks ease.

**(p-137)** **His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾.** Al-Zajjaj said: The predicate of "inna" (indeed) here has three possible forms.

The first is that it is an implied predicate, meaning ﴿Indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾, with "minhum" (from among them) implied. It was not necessary to mention "minhum" (from among them), because God, exalted is He, has already informed us that He nullifies the deeds of those who do not believe.

The second is that the predicate of "inna" is ﴿those, for them are Gardens of Eternity﴾. In this case, His saying ﴿Indeed, We do not waste﴾ is an interjected clause separating the subject from its predicate, because it contains the meaning of the first statement, since one who does good work is in the position of those who believe.

The third is that the predicate is ﴿Indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾, in the sense of: Indeed, We do not waste their reward.

The exegetes said: The meaning of ﴿We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾ is: We do not let his deeds go to waste; rather, We reward him for them with reward.

As for "al-asawir" (bracelets), al-Farra' said: For its singular form there are three dialectal variants: *iswar*, *siwar* and *suwar*. Whoever says *iswar* pluralizes it as *asawir*, and whoever says *siwar* or *suwar* pluralizes it as *asawira*. It is also possible that the singular of *asawira* and *asawir* is *siwar*. Al-Zajjaj said: *Al-asawir* is the plural of *asawira*, and *asawira* is the plural of *siwar*; it is said *siwar al-yad* (a bracelet of the hand), with a kasra, and *suwar* has also been reported. The exegetes said: Since kings in this world wore bracelets on their hands and crowns on their heads, God made that available to the people of Paradise. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Each of them will be adorned with three kinds of bracelets: one of silver, one of gold, and one of pearls and jacinths.

As for "al-sundus" (fine silk) and "al-istabraq" (thick brocade), Ibn Qutayba said: *Al-sundus* is thin brocade, and *al-istabraq* is its thick kind. I read to our teacher Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: *Al-sundus* is thin brocade. The lexicographers have not disagreed that it is a loanword (arabized). The rajiz (poet) said:

*And a night of the nights, dark-black,*
*whose borders are the color of sundus.*

**(p-138)** *Al-istabraq* is thick brocade, a Persian word arabized, and its original form is *istafreh*. Ibn Durayd said: *Istarwah*, and it was transferred from the non-Arabic language into Arabic. If *istabraq* were diminutived or broken into its plural, the diminutive would be *ubayriq*, and the broken plural would be *abariq*, with the *sin* and the *ta'* both dropped.

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿reclining therein﴾.** *Al-ittika'* (reclining) means leaning heavily upon something. Abu 'Ubayda said: *Al-ara'ik* (couches) are the furnishings within canopied enclosures, and an *arika* is only (a couch) with a canopy and a bed. Ibn Qutayba said: *Al-ara'ik* are the beds within canopied enclosures; its singular is *arika*. Tha'lab said: An *arika* is only a bed inside a pavilion, upon which are its furnishings and its household goods. Ibn Qutayba said: *Al-shawar* (furnishings) is with an open *shin*, and it means the household goods of the house. Al-Zajjaj said: *Al-ara'ik* are the furnishings within canopied enclosures. He said: It was also said that they are cushions, and it was said they are beds, and in the literal sense they are cushions that were within canopied enclosures belonging to them.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 18, verses 32–36:**

(p. 139) Allah's words: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men﴾. ʿAṭāʾ narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: They were two sons of a king among the Children of Israel. Their father died and left them. One of them acquired gardens and palaces, while the other was ascetic regarding the world. Whenever his brother acquired something of the world's adornment, he would take the like of it and send it ahead for his Hereafter, until his wealth was exhausted. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, struck them as a parable for the believer and the disbeliever whom blessing had made arrogant.

Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that when the Muslim fell into need, he approached his disbelieving brother. The disbeliever said: "Where is what you inherited from your father?" He said: "I spent it in the way of Allah." The disbeliever said: "But I bought with it gardens, sheep and cattle. By Allah, I will never give you anything until you follow my religion." Then he took the Muslim by the hand, led him into his gardens, walked him around in them, and made his religion appealing to him.

Muqatil said: The name of the believer was Yamlikha, and the name of the disbeliever was Qartas. It was also said: Qutrus. It was also said: this parable was struck for ʿUyayna ibn Hisn and his companions, and for Salman and his companions.

Allah's words: ﴿And We had surrounded the two of them with date palms﴾. Al-Ḥaff means encircling something. From it is His saying: ﴿Surrounding the Throne﴾ (Az-Zumar 39:75). The meaning is: We made the palms encompass them. His words: ﴿And We placed between them cultivated land﴾ inform that their cultivation was complete.

Allah's words: ﴿Each of the two gardens yielded its produce﴾. Al-Farraʾ said: He did not say "ātatā" (they two yielded), because kilta ("both") denotes two and its singular is not used. Its root is kull ("each/all"), just as one says kull for three. So the original rule would be that for two it takes what applies to the plural. Making it singular is permissible according to the view of kull, and feminine agreement is permissible because of the feminine marker that appears in kilta. The same applies to kullan, kilta and kulli when they are attached to a definite noun and the verb follows them: you may use the singular or the plural. Of the singular is Allah's words: ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾ (Maryam 19:95). Of the plural is: ﴿And all came to Him, humbled﴾ (An-Naml 27:87). The Arabs also do this with ayy ("which"), making it feminine or masculine. Allah says: ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾ (Luqman 31:34). It is permissible in speech to say bi-ayti arḍin ("in which land"). Likewise: (p. 140) ﴿In whatever form He willed, He assembled you﴾ (Al-Infitar 82:8). It is permissible in speech to say fī ayyati. The poet said:

*By what affliction, or by what blessing,*
*Did Muslim and al-Muhallab precede me?*

Ibn al-Anbari said: Although kilta, in meaning, refers to two, its wording is that of a feminine singular, so the wording prevailed, and the meaning was not used, trusting the addressee's knowledge of it. Among the Arabs are those who give priority to meaning over wording, saying: ﴿Each of the two gardens yielded its produce﴾ (ātatā), and others say: "āta uklahu" (it yielded its produce), because kilta conveys the meaning of kull. The poet said:

*And both of them have been inscribed for me in my record,*
*So neither death do I desire, nor life do I long for.*

He means: each of them has been inscribed for me. The Arabs have said: kullukum dhāhib ("each of you is going") and kullukum dhāhibūn ("all of you are going"). They made the word kull singular and made the plural for its meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: He did not say "ātatā," because the wording of kilta is that of a single feminine, and the meaning is: each one of them yielded its produce.

﴿And did not wrong﴾, i.e., did not diminish, ﴿anything from it. And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾: this informs us that their irrigation was from the water of a river, which is among the most abundant irrigation. Al-Farraʾ said: He said "fajjarnā" with the intensive form (shaddah), though it is one river, because a river extends, so the gushing was throughout it. Abu Razin, Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-ʿAliya, Ibn Yaʿmur and Ibn Abi ʿAbla recited "wa-fajjarnā" with the light form. Abu Mijlaz and Abu al-Mutawakkil recited "khilalahumā" (lexical variant of khilāl, "between them"). Abu al-ʿAliya and Abu ʿImran recited "nahran" with the ha' (of nahr) vowelless.

Allah's words: ﴿And he had fruit﴾, i.e., for the disbelieving brother. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited: "wa-kāna lahu thumurun" and "wa-uḥīṭa bi-thumurihi," with two ḍammas. ʿĀṣim recited: "wa-kāna lahum thamarun" and "wa-uḥīṭa bi-thamarihi," with fatḥa on the thāʾ and the mīm in both. (p. 141) Abu ʿAmr recited: "thamarun" and "bi-thamarihi," with one ḍamma and the mīm sukūn. Al-Farraʾ said: thamar with fatḥa on the thāʾ and mīm means the edible produce, and with ḍamma means wealth. Ibn al-Anbari said: thamar with fatḥa is the first plural (collective), and thamar with ḍamma is the plural of thamar. It is said: thamar and thumur, just as asad and usd. It is also possible that thamar is the plural of thimār, just as ḥimār and ḥumur, and kitāb and kutub. Whoever reads with ḍamma says: thamar is more general, because it can include edible fruits and gathered wealth. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: Abu ʿAmr's reading "thamarun" may be the plural of thimār, like kitāb and kutub, lightened so that it is said kutb; it may be that thamar is the plural of thamara, like badana and budn, and khashaba and khushb; and it may be that thumur is singular, like ʿunuq and ṭunub.

The commentators mentioned three views concerning the reading of the one who read with ḍamma:

The first: it is abundant wealth of various kinds. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is gold and silver. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: it is the plural of thamara. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said thamara, thimār and thamar.

If it is asked: What is the benefit of mentioning the fruit after mentioning the two gardens, when it is known that the owner of a garden is never without fruit? There are three answers:

The first: the land itself was not his property; only the fruits were his. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: mentioning the fruit is evidence of the abundance of what he possessed of fruits in the two gardens and elsewhere. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this.

The third: we have already said that the intended meaning of thamar is the wealth of various kinds, and we mentioned (p. 142) that it is gold and silver, and that differs from edible fruit. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: whoever says it is gold and silver, it is called thamar only as an omen, because thamar is growth in that which bears fruit, and its being here with harvest is closer than gold and silver. This is strengthened by: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to turn his palms over for what he had spent on it﴾ (Al-Kahf 18:42), and spending is with silver, not with trees.

Allah's words: ﴿Then he said﴾, i.e., the disbeliever, ﴿to his companion﴾, the believer, ﴿while he was conversing with him﴾, i.e., he was returning speech to him and answering him.

Concerning what they conversed about there are two views:

One: it is belief and disbelief.

The second: it is the seeking of the world and the seeking of the Hereafter. As for nafar, they are the group, and similar are qawm and rahṭ. [These words have no singular from their own form. Ibn Faris the lexicographer said:] nafar is a number of men from three to ten.

Concerning whom he intended by his nafar there are three views:

One: his servant (ʿUbayda). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: his children. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: his clan and his kin. This was said by Abu Sulayman.

Allah's words: ﴿And he entered his garden﴾, i.e., the disbeliever, ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ by disbelief. He had taken his brother by the hand and brought him in with him. ﴿He said: I do not think that this will ever perish﴾. He denied the perishing of the world and the perishing of his garden, and he denied the Resurrection and recompense by his saying: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾. This is doubt on his part concerning the Resurrection. Then he said: ﴿And if I should be returned to my Lord﴾, i.e., as you claim. [Ibn ʿAbbas] said: He means: if the Resurrection is true, ﴿I will surely find better than this﴾. Abu ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited: "khayran minhā" (singular). This is also how it appears in the mushafs of the people of Basra and Kufa. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir recited: "khayran minhumā" (dual), with an added mīm on the dual, and this is how it appears in the mushafs of the people of Mecca, Medina and Syria. (p. 143) Abu ʿAli said: the singular is preferable, because it is closer to the single garden in His words "and he entered his garden," and the dual is not ruled out, since the mention of the two gardens preceded.

Allah's words: ﴿as a return﴾, i.e., just as He gave him this in the world, He will give me something better than it in the Hereafter.

Allah's words: ﴿And We had surrounded the two of them with date palms﴾. Al-Ḥaff means encircling something. From it is His saying: ﴿Surrounding the Throne﴾ (Az-Zumar 39:75). The meaning is: We made the palms encompass them. His words: ﴿And We placed between them cultivated land﴾ inform that their cultivation was complete.

Allah's words: ﴿Each of the two gardens yielded its produce﴾. Al-Farraʾ said: He did not say "ātatā" (they two yielded), because kilta ("both") denotes two and its singular is not used. Its root is kull ("each/all"), just as one says kull for three. So the original rule would be that for two it takes what applies to the plural. Making it singular is permissible according to the view of kull, and feminine agreement is permissible because of the feminine marker that appears in kilta. The same applies to kullan, kilta and kulli when they are attached to a definite noun and the verb follows them: you may use the singular or the plural. Of the singular is Allah's words: ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾ (Maryam 19:95). Of the plural is: ﴿And all came to Him, humbled﴾ (An-Naml 27:87). The Arabs also do this with ayy ("which"), making it feminine or masculine. Allah says: ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾ (Luqman 31:34). It is permissible in speech to say bi-ayti arḍin ("in which land"). Likewise: (p. 140) ﴿In whatever form He willed, He assembled you﴾ (Al-Infitar 82:8). It is permissible in speech to say fī ayyati. The poet said:

*By what affliction, or by what blessing,*
*Did Muslim and al-Muhallab precede me?*

Ibn al-Anbari said: Although kilta, in meaning, refers to two, its wording is that of a feminine singular, so the wording prevailed, and the meaning was not used, trusting the addressee's knowledge of it. Among the Arabs are those who give priority to meaning over wording, saying: ﴿Each of the two gardens yielded its produce﴾ (ātatā), and others say: "āta uklahu" (it yielded its produce), because kilta conveys the meaning of kull. The poet said:

*And both of them have been inscribed for me in my record,*
*So neither death do I desire, nor life do I long for.*

He means: each of them has been inscribed for me. The Arabs have said: kullukum dhāhib ("each of you is going") and kullukum dhāhibūn ("all of you are going"). They made the word kull singular and made the plural for its meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: He did not say "ātatā," because the wording of kilta is that of a single feminine, and the meaning is: each one of them yielded its produce.

﴿And did not wrong﴾, i.e., did not diminish, ﴿anything from it. And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾: this informs us that their irrigation was from the water of a river, which is among the most abundant irrigation. Al-Farraʾ said: He said "fajjarnā" with the intensive form (shaddah), though it is one river, because a river extends, so the gushing was throughout it. Abu Razin, Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-ʿAliya, Ibn Yaʿmur and Ibn Abi ʿAbla recited "wa-fajjarnā" with the light form. Abu Mijlaz and Abu al-Mutawakkil recited "khilalahumā" (lexical variant of khilāl, "between them"). Abu al-ʿAliya and Abu ʿImran recited "nahran" with the ha' (of nahr) vowelless.

Allah's words: ﴿And he had fruit﴾, i.e., for the disbelieving brother. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited: "wa-kāna lahu thumurun" and "wa-uḥīṭa bi-thumurihi," with two ḍammas. ʿĀṣim recited: "wa-kāna lahum thamarun" and "wa-uḥīṭa bi-thamarihi," with fatḥa on the thāʾ and the mīm in both. (p. 141) Abu ʿAmr recited: "thamarun" and "bi-thamarihi," with one ḍamma and the mīm sukūn. Al-Farraʾ said: thamar with fatḥa on the thāʾ and mīm means the edible produce, and with ḍamma means wealth. Ibn al-Anbari said: thamar with fatḥa is the first plural (collective), and thamar with ḍamma is the plural of thamar. It is said: thamar and thumur, just as asad and usd. It is also possible that thamar is the plural of thimār, just as ḥimār and ḥumur, and kitāb and kutub. Whoever reads with ḍamma says: thamar is more general, because it can include edible fruits and gathered wealth. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: Abu ʿAmr's reading "thamarun" may be the plural of thimār, like kitāb and kutub, lightened so that it is said kutb; it may be that thamar is the plural of thamara, like badana and budn, and khashaba and khushb; and it may be that thumur is singular, like ʿunuq and ṭunub.

The commentators mentioned three views concerning the reading of the one who read with ḍamma:

The first: it is abundant wealth of various kinds. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is gold and silver. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: it is the plural of thamara. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said thamara, thimār and thamar.

If it is asked: What is the benefit of mentioning the fruit after mentioning the two gardens, when it is known that the owner of a garden is never without fruit? There are three answers:

The first: the land itself was not his property; only the fruits were his. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: mentioning the fruit is evidence of the abundance of what he possessed of fruits in the two gardens and elsewhere. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this.

The third: we have already said that the intended meaning of thamar is the wealth of various kinds, and we mentioned (p. 142) that it is gold and silver, and that differs from edible fruit. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: whoever says it is gold and silver, it is called thamar only as an omen, because thamar is growth in that which bears fruit, and its being here with harvest is closer than gold and silver. This is strengthened by: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to turn his palms over for what he had spent on it﴾ (Al-Kahf 18:42), and spending is with silver, not with trees.

Allah's words: ﴿Then he said﴾, i.e., the disbeliever, ﴿to his companion﴾, the believer, ﴿while he was conversing with him﴾, i.e., he was returning speech to him and answering him.

Concerning what they conversed about there are two views:

One: it is belief and disbelief.

The second: it is the seeking of the world and the seeking of the Hereafter. As for nafar, they are the group, and similar are qawm and rahṭ. [These words have no singular from their own form. Ibn Faris the lexicographer said:] nafar is a number of men from three to ten.

Concerning whom he intended by his nafar there are three views:

One: his servant (ʿUbayda). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: his children. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: his clan and his kin. This was said by Abu Sulayman.

Allah's words: ﴿And he entered his garden﴾, i.e., the disbeliever, ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ by disbelief. He had taken his brother by the hand and brought him in with him. ﴿He said: I do not think that this will ever perish﴾. He denied the perishing of the world and the perishing of his garden, and he denied the Resurrection and recompense by his saying: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾. This is doubt on his part concerning the Resurrection. Then he said: ﴿And if I should be returned to my Lord﴾, i.e., as you claim. [Ibn ʿAbbas] said: He means: if the Resurrection is true, ﴿I will surely find better than this﴾. Abu ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited: "khayran minhā" (singular). This is also how it appears in the mushafs of the people of Basra and Kufa. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir recited: "khayran minhumā" (dual), with an added mīm on the dual, and this is how it appears in the mushafs of the people of Mecca, Medina and Syria. (p. 143) Abu ʿAli said: the singular is preferable, because it is closer to the single garden in His words "and he entered his garden," and the dual is not ruled out, since the mention of the two gardens preceded.

Allah's words: ﴿as a return﴾, i.e., just as He gave him this in the world, He will give me something better than it in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verse 37–41:

His Almighty's saying: ﴿His companion said to him while he was arguing with him: "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust"﴾ — meaning Adam, your father — ﴿"then from a sperm-drop"﴾ — meaning that from which he himself was produced. So when he doubted the Resurrection, he became a disbeliever.

His Almighty's saying: ﴿"But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord"﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Qalun from Nafi' read: (لَكِنَّ هو اللَّهُ رَبِّي) with the alif dropped in pausal pronunciation (wasl) and retained in stopping (waqf). Nafi', in the narration of al-Musayyabi, read with the alif retained both in wasl and waqf. Ibn 'Amir retained the alif in both conditions. Abu Raja' read (لَكِنْ) with the nun sukun and lightened, without an alif, in both conditions. Ibn Ya'mur read (لَكِنَّ) with the nun shaddah, without an alif, in both conditions. Al-Hasan read (لَكِنَّ أنا هو اللَّهُ رَبِّي) with the nun of (لَكِنْ) sukun and the (أنا) affirmed. Al-Farra' said: "There are three dialectal forms: لَكِنّا, لَكِنْ, and لَكِنَّهُ with the hé. Abu Thirwan recited to me:

"And you strike me with your glance, saying, 'You are guilty,' and you shun me. But as for you, I do not shun you."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: its underlying form is: لَكِنَّ أنا هو اللَّهُ رَبِّي, then the first alif was dropped, and one of the two nuns was assimilated into the other, so it was doubled. Al-Zajjaj said: this alif is dropped in wasl and retained in waqf. As for the one who retains it in wasl as it is retained in waqf, it is according to the dialect of one who says "أنا قُمْتُ" (I stood), retaining the alif. The poet said:

"I am the sword of the tribe, so know me, a noble one who has raised high his eminence."

This reading is good, because the hamzah has been dropped from (أنا), so the retention of the alif becomes a substitute for the hamzah.

His Almighty's saying: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What Allah willed [has come to pass]; there is no power except in Allah"﴾? That is, "why did you not say," and the meaning of the statement is reproach. Al-Farra' said: ﴿What Allah willed﴾ is in the place of nominative case; if you wish, you raise it by supposing a pronoun (هو), meaning: [it is] what Allah willed. And if you wish, you supply within it: what Allah willed came to pass. It is permissible to omit the response of the conditional, as it is permissible in His saying: ﴿And if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 35], there being no response because it is known. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿There is no power except in Allah﴾: the preferred reading is the accusative without tanwin, as a negation, like His saying: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Kahf: 21]. It is also permissible to read ﴿there is no power except in Allah﴾ in the nominative as a subject with the predicate "bi-Allah." The meaning: no one is strong in his body or in the possession of his hand except by Allah, and he possesses nothing except what Allah willed.

His Almighty's saying: ﴿If you see me﴾. Ibn Kathir read: (إنْ تَرْنِي أنا) and (يُؤْتِيَنِي خَيْرًا) with a ya' both in wasl and waqf. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read with a ya' in wasl. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, and Hamzah read with the ya' omitted in both of them, in wasl and waqf. ﴿I am less than you in wealth and children﴾. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: (أنا أقَلُّ) with the lam in the nominative. Al-Farra' said: (أنا) here is a pronoun of separation if you put (أقَلَّ) in the accusative, and it is the subject if you put (أقَلُّ) in the nominative, and both readings are permissible.

His Almighty's saying: ﴿So it may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾; that is, in the Hereafter, ﴿and will send upon it a calamity from the heaven﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

One: it is the punishment. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah and al-Dahhak said the same. Abu Salih said from Ibn 'Abbas: fire from the sky.

Two: it is a decree from Allah which He decrees. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Three: it is projectiles from the sky, and its singular is ḥusbānah. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-ḥusbān are arrows which a man shoots from within a reed that is drawn into the bow, then he shoots twenty of them at once. According to this opinion, the meaning is: He will send upon it projectiles of His punishment, whether stones, or hail, or other kinds of punishment that He wills.

Four: that al-ḥusbān means reckoning, like His saying: ﴿The sun and the moon [move] by reckoning﴾ [al-Rahman: 5]; that is, by calculation. So the meaning becomes: He will send upon it the punishment of the reckoning of what his hands have earned. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

His Almighty's saying: ﴿So it becomes a bare, slippery earth﴾; ﴿or its water sinks away into the ground so you cannot find it.﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: al-ṣa'īd is the smooth, level ground; al-zalaq is that on which feet slip; and al-ghawr is the sunken, (p-146) so the verbal noun is made an attribute, as one says: "māʾ ghawr" (sunken water), and "miyāh ghawr," and it is not made dual, plural, or feminine, just as one says: "rajul nawm" (a man who sleeps much), "rajul ṣawm" (a man who fasts), "rajul fiṭr," and "rijāl nawm," "nisāʾ nawm," and "nisāʾ ṣawm." And it is said of women when they wail: "nawḥ." The meaning: its water goes away sunken into the earth; that is, going away into it. ﴿So you will not be able to find it by any means﴾; so no trace remains by which you could seek it, nor can hands or ropes reach it. Ibn al-Anbari said: ﴿ghawran﴾: when it sinks, the mudaf is dropped and the mudaf ilayhi takes its place, and the intended "ṭalab" here is "reaching," so the seeking stood in its place because it is its cause. Abu al-Jawza' and Abu al-Mutawakkil read: (غُؤُورًا) with the ghayn and the first waw both raised, followed by a waw.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 18, verses 42–44:**

Allah's words: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (by ruin)﴾; that is, Allah sent the punishment to encompass his fruit. The meaning of *thamar* (fruit) has already been explained. ﴿So he began to turn over his palms﴾; that is, he struck one palm against the other, and this is the action of one who regrets. ﴿Over what he had spent upon it﴾; that is, upon his garden. Here *fi* (in) carries the sense of *'ala* (upon). ﴿While it was fallen over its trellises﴾; that is, empty and collapsed. ﴿Over its trellises﴾: *al-'Uruush* means the roofs. The meaning is that its walls were still standing while its roofs had collapsed and fallen to the ground, so the walls appeared to be resting upon the roofs. ﴿And he said, "Oh, I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ Allah informs us that when He took away from him what He had bestowed upon him, and fulfilled what his brother had warned him of in this world, he regretted his polytheism at a time when regret would not benefit him. It was also said: this is what he will say on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And he had no company to support him﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read *wa lam takun* (with the *ta'*). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *wa lam yakun* (with the *ya'*). *Al-Fi'ah* means a group. ﴿Who could support him﴾; that is, who could protect him from the punishment of Allah.

Allah's words: ﴿There, protection belongs to Allah, the Truth﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read *al-Walayah* with a *fatha* on the *waw*, and *lillahi al-haqqi* with a *kasra* on the *ha'* of *lillahi* (the genitive). Hamza read *al-Walayah* with a *kasra* on the *waw*, and *lillahi al-haqqi* with a *kasra* on the *qaf* as well. Abu 'Amr read *al-Walayah* with a *fatha* on the *waw* and a *raf'* (nominative) on *al-Haqq*, and al-Kisa'i agreed with him on the *raf'* of the *qaf*, but he read *al-Wilayah* with a *kasra*. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of *al-Wilayah* in such a situation is the manifestation of the support of the friend of Allah. Others said: this statement refers back to what came before the story of the two men. As for the one who reads the *waw* of *al-Walayah* with a *fatha*, he means *al-Muwalah* (allegiance) and *al-Nusrah* (support); and whoever reads it with a *kasra* means *al-Sultan* (authority) and *al-Mulk* (dominion), as we explained at the end of *al-Anfal* (8:72). According to the *fatha* reading, there are two opinions regarding the meaning:

The first: they will take Allah as their protector on the Day of Resurrection, and will believe in Him, and will disown what they used to worship. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

The second: there, Allah will take charge of the affairs of all creation, so He will support the believers and abandon the disbelievers. According to the *kasra* reading, the meaning is: there, authority belongs to Allah. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads the *qaf* of *al-Haqq* with a *kasra* makes it an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and whoever reads it with a *raf'* makes it an attribute of *al-Walayah*.

If it is asked: why is *al-Walayah* described as *al-Haqq*, given that *al-Walayah* is feminine while *al-Haqq* is a verbal noun (*masdar*)? There are two answers to this, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari:

The first: its feminine form is not a true feminine, so it was treated according to the meaning of *al-Nasr* (support). The implied meaning is: there, support belongs to Allah, the Truth, just as *al-Sayhah* (the cry) was treated according to the meaning of *al-Siyah* (the shouting) in His words: ﴿And the blast seized those who had wronged﴾ [Hud: 67].

The second: *al-Haqq* is a verbal noun whose form is the same for the masculine, the feminine, the singular, the dual and the plural. So it is said: "your statement is *haqq*," "your word is *haqq*," and "your sayings are *haqq*." It is also permissible for *al-Haqq* to be in the nominative, as a praise of *al-Walayah*, and as a praise of Allah, Exalted, by implying *huwa* (He).

Allah's words: ﴿He is best in reward﴾; that is, He is better in reward than whoever is hoped to reward, and this is on the assumption that if anyone else were to reward, his reward would be the better.

Allah's words: ﴿And best in outcome﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read *'Uqban* with a *damma* on the *qaf*. 'Asim and Hamza read *'Uqban* with the *qaf* unvowelled (sukun). Abu 'Ali said: whatever is of the form *fi'l* (such as *'unuq* and *tunub*) may be lightened. Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-'Uqub*, *al-'Uqb*, *al-'Uqba* and *al-'Aqibah* have the same meaning, namely the final end. The meaning is: the outcome of obeying Allah is better than the outcome of obeying anyone else.

The meaning is: the outcome of obeying Allah is better than the outcome of obeying anyone else.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 18, verses 42–44:**

Allah's words: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (by ruin)﴾; that is, Allah sent the punishment to encompass his fruit. The meaning of *thamar* (fruit) has already been explained. ﴿So he began to turn over his palms﴾; that is, he struck one palm against the other, and this is the action of one who regrets. ﴿Over what he had spent upon it﴾; that is, upon his garden. Here *fi* (in) carries the sense of *'ala* (upon). ﴿While it was fallen over its trellises﴾; that is, empty and collapsed. ﴿Over its trellises﴾: *al-'Uruush* means the roofs. The meaning is that its walls were still standing while its roofs had collapsed and fallen to the ground, so the walls appeared to be resting upon the roofs. ﴿And he said, "Oh, I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ Allah informs us that when He took away from him what He had bestowed upon him, and fulfilled what his brother had warned him of in this world, he regretted his polytheism at a time when regret would not benefit him. It was also said: this is what he will say on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And he had no company to support him﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read *wa lam takun* (with the *ta'*). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *wa lam yakun* (with the *ya'*). *Al-Fi'ah* means a group. ﴿Who could support him﴾; that is, who could protect him from the punishment of Allah.

Allah's words: ﴿There, protection belongs to Allah, the Truth﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read *al-Walayah* with a *fatha* on the *waw*, and *lillahi al-haqqi* with a *kasra* on the *ha'* of *lillahi* (the genitive). Hamza read *al-Walayah* with a *kasra* on the *waw*, and *lillahi al-haqqi* with a *kasra* on the *qaf* as well. Abu 'Amr read *al-Walayah* with a *fatha* on the *waw* and a *raf'* (nominative) on *al-Haqq*, and al-Kisa'i agreed with him on the *raf'* of the *qaf*, but he read *al-Wilayah* with a *kasra*. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of *al-Wilayah* in such a situation is the manifestation of the support of the friend of Allah. Others said: this statement refers back to what came before the story of the two men. As for the one who reads the *waw* of *al-Walayah* with a *fatha*, he means *al-Muwalah* (allegiance) and *al-Nusrah* (support); and whoever reads it with a *kasra* means *al-Sultan* (authority) and *al-Mulk* (dominion), as we explained at the end of *al-Anfal* (8:72). According to the *fatha* reading, there are two opinions regarding the meaning:

The first: they will take Allah as their protector on the Day of Resurrection, and will believe in Him, and will disown what they used to worship. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

The second: there, Allah will take charge of the affairs of all creation, so He will support the believers and abandon the disbelievers. According to the *kasra* reading, the meaning is: there, authority belongs to Allah. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads the *qaf* of *al-Haqq* with a *kasra* makes it an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and whoever reads it with a *raf'* makes it an attribute of *al-Walayah*.

If it is asked: why is *al-Walayah* described as *al-Haqq*, given that *al-Walayah* is feminine while *al-Haqq* is a verbal noun (*masdar*)? There are two answers to this, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari:

The first: its feminine form is not a true feminine, so it was treated according to the meaning of *al-Nasr* (support). The implied meaning is: there, support belongs to Allah, the Truth, just as *al-Sayhah* (the cry) was treated according to the meaning of *al-Siyah* (the shouting) in His words: ﴿And the blast seized those who had wronged﴾ [Hud: 67].

The second: *al-Haqq* is a verbal noun whose form is the same for the masculine, the feminine, the singular, the dual and the plural. So it is said: "your statement is *haqq*," "your word is *haqq*," and "your sayings are *haqq*." It is also permissible for *al-Haqq* to be in the nominative, as a praise of *al-Walayah*, and as a praise of Allah, Exalted, by implying *huwa* (He).

Allah's words: ﴿He is best in reward﴾; that is, He is better in reward than whoever is hoped to reward, and this is on the assumption that if anyone else were to reward, his reward would be the better.

Allah's words: ﴿And best in outcome﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read *'Uqban* with a *damma* on the *qaf*. 'Asim and Hamza read *'Uqban* with the *qaf* unvowelled (sukun). Abu 'Ali said: whatever is of the form *fi'l* (such as *'unuq* and *tunub*) may be lightened. Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-'Uqub*, *al-'Uqb*, *al-'Uqba* and *al-'Aqibah* have the same meaning, namely the final end. The meaning is: the outcome of obeying Allah is better than the outcome of obeying anyone else.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verse 45:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And set forth for them the example of the life of this world﴾; that is, in the swiftness of its passing and its going away. It was also said: in the changing of its conditions, for with every joy there is a sorrow. This has been explained in Surah Yunus (24), up to His saying: ﴿So it becomes dry stubble﴾. Al-Farra' said: al-Hashim (the dry stubble) is everything that was moist and then dried out. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Hashim is dry vegetation. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-Hashim from plants is that which has crumbled, and its root is from "I crushed the thing" (hashamtu al-shay'), meaning when you break it; and from it the man was named Hashim. ﴿Which the winds scatter﴾ means they blow it away. Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: (tudhrihi), with a raised taa' (tu-), a kasra on the raa' after it, a silent yaa' and a kasra on the haa' (tudhriihi, with the pronoun). Ibn Mas'ud read the same way, except that he put a fatha on the taa'. Al-Muqtadir is of the form mufta'il, from qadartu (I had power). The exegetes said: ﴿And Allah is over all things﴾ in regard to bringing into being and bringing to an end, ﴿Capable (muqtadiran)﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verse 46:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life﴾. This is a rebuttal of the polytheists who used to boast of their wealth and children. God Exalted informs that these are among the things one adorns oneself with in this world, [not] among the things that benefit in the Hereafter.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾. Concerning them there are five opinions:

The first: they are "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest." Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "If you are unable to stay awake at night to exert yourselves in worship, and unable to fight the enemy, then do not be unable to say: Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest. Say them, for they are the enduring good deeds." This is the view of Ibn Abbas in the narration of Ata', and Mujahid, Ata', Ikrimah and al-Dahhak held it. Uthman ibn Affan (may God be pleased with him) was asked about the enduring good deeds, and he said: these words, and he added to them: "There is no power and no strength except with God." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said the same, precisely.

The second: they are "There is no god but God, God is greatest, praise be to God, and there is no power except with God." This was related by Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

The third: they are the five daily prayers. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related it from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq and Ibrahim said the same.

The fourth: good speech. al-Awfi related it from Ibn Abbas.

The fifth: they are all good deeds. Ibn Abi Talhah related it from Ibn Abbas, and Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said the same.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Better in the sight of your Lord for reward﴾; that is, better in recompense. ﴿And better in hope﴾; that is, better than what you hope for, because your hopes are false, whereas this hope does not deceive.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verse 47–51:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read: (wa-yawma tusayyaru) with the ta' (tā'), and (al-jibālu) in the nominative (raf'an). Nafi', 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: (nusayyiru) with the nun, and (al-jibāla) in the accusative (naṣban). Ibn Muhaysin read: (wa-yawma tasīru) with a fatha on the ta', a kasra on the sin, and a sukun on the ya', (al-jibālu) in the nominative. Al-Zajjaj said: (wa-yawma) is in the accusative by the sense of (udhkur, "remember"). It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as in: "And the enduring good deeds are better than a day on which the mountains move" (p-151).

Ibn 'Abbas said: The mountains will move from the surface of the earth as the clouds move in this world, then they will be crushed and will become in the earth as they came out of it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾. 'Amr ibn al-'As, Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Abu al-'Aliyah read: (wa-turā al-arḍu bāriza) with a raf' on the ta' and the ḍād. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read likewise, except that he put a fatha on the ḍād of (al-arḍi).

Regarding the meaning of ﴿bāriza﴾ there are two opinions: One is [apparent], that nothing of mountain, tree or building is upon it; this is said by most. The second: its people will be brought forth from its belly; this is said by al-Farra'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gather them﴾, meaning the believers and the disbelievers, ﴿and leave none of them behind﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, We do not leave anyone behind. It is said: "ghadartu kadhā" means "I left such-and-such behind," and from it the word ghadīr (pond) derives, because it is water that the floods leave behind. Aban narrated (fa-lam tughādir) with the ta'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾. If it is said: this is a future matter, so how is it expressed in the past tense? The answer: what Allah has known will occur is treated as though it is witnessed, like His saying: "And the companions of Paradise will call out" (al-A'raf: 43).

Regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿ṣaffan﴾ there are four opinions:

One: it means "all together," as in His saying: "Then come in rows" (Ta-Ha: 64); this is said by Muqatil.

The second: the meaning is: they will be presented before your Lord arranged in lines; this is the position of the Basrans.

The third: the meaning is: they will be presented before your Lord in rows, and the singular stands in for the plural, as in His saying: "Then We bring you forth as a child" (al-Hajj: 5).

The fourth: none of them will be hidden from Allah, so they are like a row whose entirety is easy to encompass. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these opinions. It has been said that every nation and group is a row (ṣaff).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you have come to Us﴾. There is an implied element here (fa-yuqalu lahum, "so it will be said to them").

Regarding who is addressed by this there are two opinions: One: they are all of them. The second: the disbelievers, so the wording is general and the meaning is specific. His saying: ﴿as We created you the first time﴾ is explained in (al-An'am: 94). His saying: ﴿Rather, you claimed﴾ is an address to the disbelievers specifically, and the meaning is: you claimed in the world ﴿that We would never make for you an appointment﴾ for resurrection and recompense.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the Book will be placed﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions:

One: it is the Book in which what creatures will do before their existence was inscribed; this is said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is the reckoning; this is said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The third: it is the Book of deeds; this is said by Muqatil. Ibn Jarir said: He placed the book of the servants' deeds in their hands, so according to this the word "Book" is a generic noun.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So you will see the criminals﴾. Mujahid said: they are the disbelievers. Some scholars mentioned that every "criminal" (mujrim) mentioned in the Qur'an means the disbeliever.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fearful﴾; that is, afraid ﴿of what is in it﴾ of wicked deeds, ﴿and they will say, "Woe to us!"﴾. This is the saying of everyone who falls into ruin. We have explained this meaning in His saying: "Oh, our regret!" (al-An'am: 31).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It leaves nothing small or great but that it has enumerated it﴾. This is upon its outward meaning concerning small and great matters. 'Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the small (ṣaghīra) is the smile, and the great (kabīra) is the loud laughter. It may be supposed that what is meant by this is minor and major sins, but that is not so, since smiling and laughing in themselves are not sins; rather what is meant is that smiling is among minor actions while laughing is a major action. Al-Ḍaḥḥak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the small is smiling and mocking the believers, and the great is loud laughter (p-153) at that; according to this, it is a sin among sins by reason of the intention of its doer, not in itself. The meaning of ﴿aḥṣāhā﴾ is: counted it and recorded it, and the meaning is: it was found enumerated. ﴿And they will find what they did present﴾; that is, written and recorded in the Book. It has been said: they will see its recompense present. Abu Sulayman said: the correct view according to the verifiers is that the minor sins of believers who were promised pardon for them when they avoid major sins are only pardoned in the Hereafter after their owner has seen them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾. Abu Sulayman said: the good deeds of the believer are not diminished and the evil deeds of the disbeliever are not increased. It has been said: if the disbeliever has done a good deed, such as freeing a slave or giving charity, his punishment is lightened by it; and if a Muslim wrongs him, Allah takes from the Muslim and the right becomes Allah's.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, commanded His Prophet ﴿ﷺ﴾ to mention to those arrogant ones who scorned sitting with the poor the story of Iblis and what pride inherited him. So He said: ﴿And when We said﴾; that is, remember that.

Regarding His saying ﴿he was of the jinn﴾ there are two opinions:

One: he was truly of the jinn, by this text; those who hold this argue that he has offspring, and the angels have no offspring, and that he disbelieved, while the angels are the messengers of Allah and are protected from disbelief.

The second: he was of the angels, and he was only called ﴿of the jinn﴾ because he was from a category of angels called the jinn; this is said by Ibn 'Abbas. We have explained this in (al-Baqarah: 34).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he defied the command of his Lord﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions:

One: he departed from the obedience of his Lord; the Arabs say: "fasaqat al-rutabah min qishriha" when it comes out of its skin; this is said by al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: defiance came upon him when he was commanded and disobeyed, so the cause of his defiance was the command of his Lord. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the position of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and it is the truth in our view.

The third: he defied by rejecting the command of his Lord; al-Zajjaj related this from Qutrub.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies besides Me?﴾; that is: you make them your allies by obeying them. al-Hasan and Qatadah said: his offspring are his children, and they multiply as the children of Adam multiply. Mujahid said: his offspring are the devils, and among his offspring is Zalanbur, the bearer of Iblis's banner in every market and ruin, who is the bringer of calamities; al-A'war, the companion of showing off; Miswat, the companion of rumours, who brings them and casts them onto people's mouths so that no source for them is found; and Dasim, who accompanies a man when he enters his house without greeting or mentioning the name of Allah, and eats with him when he eats. Some scholars said: if a man's sin is through pride, do not hope for him, but if it is through desire, then hope for him, for the disobedience of Iblis was through pride, and the disobedience of Adam was through desire.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions: One: wretched is the taking of them as allies for the wrongdoers. The second: wretched is Satan. The third: wretched are Satan and the offspring; these were mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read: (mā ashhadnāhum) with a nun and an alif.

Regarding those referred to there are four opinions: One: Iblis and his offspring. The second: the angels. The third: all the disbelievers. The fourth: all creation. The meaning is: I did not consult them about their creation, and in this is a demonstration of independence from helpers and a manifestation of perfect power. (p-155)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor the creation of themselves﴾; that is: I did not make some of them witness the creation of others, nor did I seek the help of some of them in bringing others into being.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I would not have taken the misleaders as helpers﴾ [meaning: the devils], ﴿as supporters﴾; that is: helpers and aides. The word "'adud" is used often in the sense of help, because it is the support of the hand [arm]. Al-Zajjaj said: al-i'tiḍād is strengthening oneself and seeking assistance; it is said: "I'taḍadtu bi-fulān," meaning: I sought his help.

Regarding what the denial of taking them as "'adud" refers to, there are two opinions: One: it is the guardianships, meaning: I would not be a guardian of the misleaders; this is said by Mujahid. The second: it is the creation of the heavens and the earth; this is said by Muqatil. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari and Abu Ja'far read: (wa-mā kuntu) with a fatha on the ta'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It leaves nothing small or great but that it has enumerated it﴾. This is upon its outward meaning concerning small and great matters. 'Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the small (ṣaghīra) is the smile, and the great (kabīra) is the loud laughter. It may be supposed that what is meant by this is minor and major sins, but that is not so, since smiling and laughing in themselves are not sins; rather what is meant is that smiling is among minor actions while laughing is a major action. Al-Ḍaḥḥak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the small is smiling and mocking the believers, and the great is loud laughter (p-153) at that; according to this, it is a sin among sins by reason of the intention of its doer, not in itself. The meaning of ﴿aḥṣāhā﴾ is: counted it and recorded it, and the meaning is: it was found enumerated. ﴿And they will find what they did present﴾; that is, written and recorded in the Book. It has been said: they will see its recompense present. Abu Sulayman said: the correct view according to the verifiers is that the minor sins of believers who were promised pardon for them when they avoid major sins are only pardoned in the Hereafter after their owner has seen them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾. Abu Sulayman said: the good deeds of the believer are not diminished and the evil deeds of the disbeliever are not increased. It has been said: if the disbeliever has done a good deed, such as freeing a slave or giving charity, his punishment is lightened by it; and if a Muslim wrongs him, Allah takes from the Muslim and the right becomes Allah's.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, commanded His Prophet ﴿ﷺ﴾ to mention to those arrogant ones who scorned sitting with the poor the story of Iblis and what pride inherited him. So He said: ﴿And when We said﴾; that is, remember that.

Regarding His saying ﴿he was of the jinn﴾ there are two opinions:

One: he was truly of the jinn, by this text; those who hold this argue that he has offspring, and the angels have no offspring, and that he disbelieved, while the angels are the messengers of Allah and are protected from disbelief.

The second: he was of the angels, and he was only called ﴿of the jinn﴾ because he was from a category of angels called the jinn; this is said by Ibn 'Abbas. We have explained this in (al-Baqarah: 34).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he defied the command of his Lord﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions:

One: he departed from the obedience of his Lord; the Arabs say: "fasaqat al-rutabah min qishriha" when it comes out of its skin; this is said by al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: defiance came upon him when he was commanded and disobeyed, so the cause of his defiance was the command of his Lord. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the position of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and it is the truth in our view.

The third: he defied by rejecting the command of his Lord; al-Zajjaj related this from Qutrub.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies besides Me?﴾; that is: you make them your allies by obeying them. al-Hasan and Qatadah said: his offspring are his children, and they multiply as the children of Adam multiply. Mujahid said: his offspring are the devils, and among his offspring is Zalanbur, the bearer of Iblis's banner in every market and ruin, who is the bringer of calamities; al-A'war, the companion of showing off; Miswat, the companion of rumours, who brings them and casts them onto people's mouths so that no source for them is found; and Dasim, who accompanies a man when he enters his house without greeting or mentioning the name of Allah, and eats with him when he eats. Some scholars said: if a man's sin is through pride, do not hope for him, but if it is through desire, then hope for him, for the disobedience of Iblis was through pride, and the disobedience of Adam was through desire.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions: One: wretched is the taking of them as allies for the wrongdoers. The second: wretched is Satan. The third: wretched are Satan and the offspring; these were mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read: (mā ashhadnāhum) with a nun and an alif.

Regarding those referred to there are four opinions: One: Iblis and his offspring. The second: the angels. The third: all the disbelievers. The fourth: all creation. The meaning is: I did not consult them about their creation, and in this is a demonstration of independence from helpers and a manifestation of perfect power. (p-155)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor the creation of themselves﴾; that is: I did not make some of them witness the creation of others, nor did I seek the help of some of them in bringing others into being.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I would not have taken the misleaders as helpers﴾ [meaning: the devils], ﴿as supporters﴾; that is: helpers and aides. The word "'adud" is used often in the sense of help, because it is the support of the hand [arm]. Al-Zajjaj said: al-i'tiḍād is strengthening oneself and seeking assistance; it is said: "I'taḍadtu bi-fulān," meaning: I sought his help.

Regarding what the denial of taking them as "'adud" refers to, there are two opinions: One: it is the guardianships, meaning: I would not be a guardian of the misleaders; this is said by Mujahid. The second: it is the creation of the heavens and the earth; this is said by Muqatil. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari and Abu Ja'far read: (wa-mā kuntu) with a fatha on the ta'.

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 18, verses 52–53:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] the Day He will say, "Call upon My partners, whom you claimed."﴾ Hamza recited *naqūlu* (﴿We will say﴾) with the letter nūn. He means: on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Call upon My partners﴾: He attributed the partners to Himself according to their (the disbelievers') assumption. The intended meaning is that they should call upon them to ward off the punishment from you or to intercede for you. ﴿Whom you claimed﴾: that is, you claimed them to be partners. ﴿So they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them﴾: that is, they will not answer them. ﴿And We will place between them﴾: regarding those referred to, there are two opinions:

The first: they are the polytheists and their partners. The second: they are the people of guidance and the people of misguidance.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿mawbiqan﴾ (a place of destruction), there are six opinions:

The first: a place of destruction. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak. Ibn Qutaybah said: a place of destruction between them and their gods in Hell. From this one says: "His sins destroyed him" (awbaqathu dhunūbuhu), that is, "they ruined him." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: We placed between them a punishment that would destroy them, that is, would ruin them. Thus *al-mawbiq* is "the place of ruin." One says: *wabaqa*, *yabiqu*, *yābiqa*, *wabqan*, *wabaqa*, *yabiqu*, *wubūqan*, so he is *wābiq* (ruined). Al-Farrāʾ said: We made their mutual connection in this world a place of ruin for them in the Hereafter. On this view, "between" (*bayn*) carries the sense of "connection," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Surely your bond has been severed﴾ (6:94), according to the recitation of those who read the nūn with a ḍammah.

The second: *al-mawbiq* is a deep valley by which the people of misguidance and the people of guidance are separated. This is the view of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr.

The third: it is a valley in Hell. This is the view of Anas ibn Malik and Mujahid.

The fourth: the meaning of *mawbiq* is enmity. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The fifth: it is a place of confinement. This is the view of al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas.

The sixth: it is a place of appointment. This is the view of Abu ʿUbayda.

Ibn al-Anbari said: If it is asked, "Why did He say *mawbiqan* (with a fatḥah on the mīm) and not *mūbiqan* (with a ḍammah on the mīm), since its meaning is 'a destroying punishment'?" The answer is: it is a noun assigned to a place of confinement in the Fire, and nouns are not derived by analogy. It is known that *mawbiqan* is a *mafʿil* form, from *awbaqahu Allah*, meaning "God destroyed him." So the mīm takes a fatḥah, as in *mawʿid*, *mawlid* and *maḥtid*, when you name persons by them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the guilty will see the Fire﴾: that is, they will witness it while it roars with rage against them. The guilty here refers to the disbelievers. ﴿So they will be certain﴾: that is, they will be certain ﴿that they are going to fall into it﴾: that is, they will be entering it. The meaning of *muwāqaʿah* (falling into) is the thing's close engagement with force. ﴿And they will not find from it any escape﴾: that is, no means of turning away. *Maṣraf* means the place to which one turns. This is because it will surround them from every side, so they will not be able to flee.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verses 54–55:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly varied in this Qur'an [every kind of example]﴾. We have explained it in (Bani Isra'il: 41).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But man is ever most disputatious﴾. There are two views concerning who this verse was revealed about:

One: it was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and his disputing was about the Qur'an. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and his disputing was about the Resurrection, when he brought a bone that had crumbled (rumma) and said: "Will Allah bring this back to life?" This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Al-Zajjaj said: "Everything that has understanding among the angels and the jinn argues, and man is the most disputatious of these beings."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them, except that there should come to them the way of the former peoples﴾. The exegetes said: it means the people of Makkah. ﴿When guidance came to them﴾ means Muhammad (ﷺ), the Qur'an and Islam. ﴿Except that there should come to them the way of the former peoples﴾ means that if they do not believe, they will be punished.

On the meaning of the statement there are three views:

One: nothing prevented them from faith except their demand that the way of the former peoples should come upon them. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: Satan prevented the people from believing, except so that the way of the former peoples would come upon them; that is, he prevented them from right guidance so that punishment would befall them. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The third: nothing prevented them except that I have decreed punishment for them. This verse concerns those among the polytheists who were killed at Badr and Uhud. This was said by al-Wahidi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or the punishment come upon them﴾. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned three views concerning "or" (aw) here:

One: it has the meaning of "and" (waw).

The second: it indicates that one of the two things occurs, since there is no benefit in specifying which.

The third: it is used for partitive meaning (tab'id), that is, that some of them will be struck by this. These three views have already been explained by us in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Qubulan﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited it as qibalan (قِبَلًا), with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba'. 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited it as qubulan (قُبُلًا), with a damma on both the qaf and the ba'. We have already explained the reasoning behind the two readings in (al-An'am: 111). Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud recited it as qabalan (قَبَلًا), with a fatha on the qaf and without a yā'. Ibn Qutayba said: it means "face to face" (isti'nafan).

If it is said: if the meaning of "the way of the former peoples" is the punishment, what is the benefit of repeating it with His saying: ﴿Or the punishment come upon them﴾?

The answer: "the way of the former peoples" conveys an indefinite punishment whose time may be delayed and whose kinds may vary, while the punishment coming "qubulan" conveys killing on the Day of Badr. Muqatil said: ﴿The way of the former peoples﴾ is the punishment of the earlier nations; ﴿or the punishment come upon them qubulan﴾ means openly (ʿayānan), killing by the sword on the Day of Badr.

(p-158)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 18, verses 56–59:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve dispute by means of falsehood﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means the mockers (al-mustahzi'in), the partitioners (al-muqtasimin) and their followers. Their disputation by means of falsehood is that they obligated him to bring signs according to their desires. ﴿That they may refute thereby the truth﴾; that is, that they may nullify what Muhammad ﷺ brought. It was also said: their disputation is their saying: ﴿When we are bones and crumbled remains?﴾ [al-Isra: 49], ﴿When we have strayed into the earth?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10], and similar statements, in order to nullify thereby what came in the Qur'an concerning the resurrection (al-ba'th) and the recompense (al-jaza'). Abu ʿUbayda said: The meaning of ﴿to refute﴾ is: to remove and eliminate. It is said: a place is slippery (dahd), that is, a slippery place in which no foot or hoof remains firm.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they take My signs﴾ meaning: the Qur'an. ﴿And what they are warned﴾; that is, what they are warned of by it, of the Fire and the Resurrection, ﴿in mockery﴾; that is, made an object of mockery.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And who is more unjust﴾. We have explained this expression in (al-Baqarah: 114). And ﴿reminded﴾ means: admonished. The signs of his Lord: the Qur'an, and turning away from them: neglecting them. ﴿And forgets what his hands have put forth﴾; that is, the sins that preceded. We have explained what follows this in (al-An'am: 21), up to His saying: ﴿And if you call them to guidance﴾, which is faith and the Qur'an, ﴿they will never be guided﴾. This is a report of His knowledge concerning them.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy﴾, in that He does not hasten to punish them. ﴿Rather, for them is an appointed time﴾ for the resurrection and recompense, ﴿they will never find beside Him a refuge﴾. Al-Farra' said: al-mawil is al-manja (a place of escape), and it is in meaning a place of refuge, because a place of escape is a refuge. The Arabs say: "He yuwali to his place," that is, he goes to his place. The poet said:

"Lā wa'alat nafsuka khallaytahā lil-ʿāmiriyyīna wa-lam tukallami"

He means: may your soul not escape. Abu ʿUbayda recited for al-A'sha:

"Wa-qad ukhālisu rabba al-bayti ghaflatahu ∗∗∗ wa-qad yuhādhiru minnī thumma mā yaʾilu"

That is: what does not escape. Ibn Qutayba said: al-mawil is al-malja' (refuge). It is said: "Wa'ala fulan ila kadha" when he took refuge.

If it is said: the apparent meaning of this verse implies that the postponement of punishment from the disbelievers is by Allah's mercy, and it is known that they have no share in His mercy?

There are two answers to this. The first: the mercy here means blessing (ni'mah), and no believer or disbeliever is free of Allah's blessing. As for the mercy which is forgiveness and good pleasure, the disbeliever has no share in it. The second: Allah's mercy is forbidden to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, but in this world they receive from it well-being and provision.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those towns﴾; he means those whose account We have related to you, and what is meant is their people; therefore He said: ﴿We destroyed them﴾. What is meant is the people of Hud and Salih, and Lut and Shu'ayb. Al-Farra' said: His saying ﴿when they wronged﴾ means: after they had been wronged.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We appointed for their destruction﴾. Most readers recited it with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam. Al-Zajjaj said: In this there are two aspects:

The first: that it is a verbal noun (masdar), so the meaning is: "and We appointed for their destruction."

The second: that it is a time, so the meaning is: "for the time of their destruction."

Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, recited it with a fatha on the mim and the lam, and it is a masdar like al-halak. Hafs, from ʿAsim, recited it with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam, and its meaning is: "for the time of their destruction."
